ox: Correct. Intersectionality (Crenshaw) says overlapping identities such as race, gender, and class interact, creating experiences that are not just the sum of each part.
Wrong. Saying each inequality works independently denies the interaction at the heart of the concept.
Wrong. Intersectionality covers several interacting categories, not only economics.
Wrong. Intersectionality sees race as socially constructed, not biologically fixed.

p: Intersectionality is the idea that a person's social categories, such as race, gender, and class, overlap and interact. Kimberle Crenshaw introduced the term.
The result is a distinct experience of disadvantage or privilege. For example, a Black woman may face discrimination that differs from what Black men or white women face.

mem: Coined by Crenshaw.
Identities overlap and interact; effects are not simply additive.
Race and gender are social constructs.
d_10A_17.trap: Treating each category as a separate, additive layer.
d_10A_17.plain: Mixing blue and yellow paint doesn't give you a bit of blue and a bit of yellow. It gives green, something new.

ox: Wrong. Families are not what Marx's concept addresses. Alienation is about the workplace.
Wrong. Marx focuses on estrangement within production, not from the government.
Correct. Under capitalism workers lack control over their labor, the products they make, fellow workers, and their human potential.
Wrong. Estrangement from norms sounds like anomie (Durkheim), a different idea.

p: Alienation means workers feel estranged because they do not control their work. They sell their labor to owners and do not own what they make.
Marx described four parts: alienation from the product, from the work process, from fellow workers, and from human potential. It comes from the economic structure, not a personal mood.

mem: Alienation: from labor, product, coworkers, human potential.
Caused by capitalist production.
Do not confuse with Durkheim's anomie.
d_10A_34.trap: Treating alienation as a mood rather than a result of how work is organized.
d_10A_34.plain: A kid who builds a toy on an assembly line and never gets to see or play with it would feel disconnected from the work.

ox: Wrong. Evidence does not support fixed innate ability differences between classes. This is a biological-determinism trap.
Wrong. Poor families generally value education highly. Blaming their values is a cultural-deficit trap.
Wrong. School start age does not explain class gaps.
Correct. Unequal school funding, plus differences in family resources, give advantages that sociologists see as the main source of class gaps.

p: Sociologists look at structure: wealthier districts fund schools through local property taxes, so rich areas get better resources.
Family resources such as books, tutoring, and stable housing add to this. Gaps arise from unequal opportunity, not lack of talent or interest.

mem: Structural resource gaps explain class differences.
School funding often depends on local property taxes.
Avoid deficit explanations.
d_10A_37.trap: Blaming individual or cultural deficits rather than structural resource differences.
d_10A_37.plain: Two kids race, but one gets good shoes and a smooth track. The gap comes from the gear, not from the kids.

ox: Correct. Residential segregation is the spatial separation of groups into different neighborhoods within the same area.
Wrong. Gentrification is higher-income newcomers moving in and displacing residents. It is a process of change, not a separation pattern.
Wrong. Suburbanization is the movement of people from cities to suburbs.
Wrong. Urban renewal is redevelopment of city areas, often clearing old housing.

p: Residential segregation is a pattern in which racial or ethnic groups live in different neighborhoods of the same metropolitan area.
It was produced historically by discriminatory lending, zoning, and housing choices, and it shapes access to schools, jobs, and services.

mem: Residential segregation: groups separated by neighborhood.
Gentrification: affluent newcomers displace residents.
Redlining and discriminatory lending helped create segregation.
x10A_001.trap: Choosing gentrification because it also changes neighborhoods.
x10A_001.plain: If every grade in a school ate lunch only at separate tables, the room would be segregated by seating.

ox: Wrong. Anti-gentrification organizing concerns displacement by rising costs, not pollution siting. The trap is picking a poor-neighborhood issue that is the wrong one.
Correct. Environmental justice addresses the unequal distribution of environmental hazards by race and class.
Wrong. Meritocracy is about assigning positions by talent and effort, not about where hazards are placed.
Wrong. Deinstitutionalization is moving psychiatric patients out of institutions into the community.

p: Environmental justice is a movement that argues environmental benefits and burdens should be shared fairly. Waste sites, highways, and polluting plants are often placed in poor and minority communities.
This is sometimes called environmental racism when race drives the pattern.

mem: Environmental justice: unequal exposure to hazards by race and class.
Gentrification: displacement through rising costs.
Deinstitutionalization: closing psychiatric institutions.
x10A_002.trap: Choosing anti-gentrification because both involve poor neighborhoods.
x10A_002.plain: If the only trash dump in town were always built next to the same neighborhood, that wouldn't be fair, and people would speak up.

ox: Wrong. No known DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to a 5' end. The direction is 5' to 3'. Trap: confusing the direction of the template read with the direction of the new strand.
Correct. DNA polymerase adds each new nucleotide to the free 3'-OH of the growing strand. So the new strand grows 5' to 3'. It reads the template 3' to 5'.
Wrong. Both leading and lagging strands are built 5' to 3'. The lagging strand just has to be built in short Okazaki fragments away from the fork.
Wrong. DNA polymerase cannot start from nothing. It needs a primer, made of RNA by primase, to provide a free 3'-OH.

p: DNA strands have two different ends, called 5' and 3'. DNA polymerase can only attach a new nucleotide to the 3' end of an existing strand. So the new strand always grows from 5' toward 3'.
It also cannot start on its own. It needs a short RNA primer that gives it a 3'-OH to build on.

mem: New DNA is made 5' to 3'
Polymerase needs a primer with a free 3'-OH
Lagging strand makes Okazaki fragments
q7.trap: Mixing up the template direction (read 3' to 5') with the direction of new synthesis (5' to 3').
q7.plain: Building a train where you can only add cars to the back. You can never add to the front, and you need a first car already in place.

ox: Wrong. Helicase unwinds the double helix. That unwinding is what creates the positive supercoils ahead of the fork. Trap: helicase causes the problem; it does not fix it.
Correct. Topoisomerase cuts one or both DNA strands, lets the DNA swivel to release tension, and then reseals the cut. This relieves the supercoiling.
Wrong. Ligase seals nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone, such as between Okazaki fragments. It does not release twisting strain.
Wrong. Primase makes short RNA primers so that polymerase can start. It has no role in supercoiling.

p: When helicase unwinds a stretch of DNA, the DNA ahead gets overwound and tight. This is called positive supercoiling. If it builds up, replication stalls.
Topoisomerase solves this. It briefly cuts the DNA, lets it spin to relax, and reseals it. In bacteria, gyrase is a topoisomerase targeted by some antibiotics.

mem: Helicase unwinds
Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling by cutting and rejoining
Primase makes RNA primers; ligase seals nicks
q8.trap: Picking helicase because it is at the fork. It creates the strain; topoisomerase removes it.
q8.plain: If you pull two twisted rope strands apart, the rope ahead of you gets twisted tighter. Someone has to snip, untwist, and tie it back.

ox: Wrong. A silent mutation changes the codon but still codes for the same amino acid. UAG codes for no amino acid, so this is not silent.
Wrong. Missense means a different amino acid is inserted. Here no amino acid is inserted. UAG is a stop signal.
Correct. UAG is a stop codon. Changing UAC (Tyr) to UAG ends translation early, so the protein is truncated. That is a nonsense mutation.
Wrong. A frameshift comes from adding or removing bases (not in multiples of 3), shifting every codon after it. Here one base was swapped, so the frame is intact.

p: A codon is three RNA bases that code for one amino acid. A point mutation swaps one base. Silent: same amino acid. Missense: different amino acid. Nonsense: a stop codon appears.
The stop codons are UAA, UAG, and UGA. If one appears early, translation ends early and the protein is shorter, usually non-functional.

mem: Stop codons: UAA, UAG, UGA
Silent: same amino acid; missense: different; nonsense: stop
Frameshift needs an insertion or deletion not divisible by 3
q9.mn: Stop codons: 'U Are Away, U Are Gone, U Go Away' for UAA, UAG, UGA.
q9.trap: Calling it missense because one amino acid is replaced. Here it is replaced by a stop signal, not another amino acid.
q9.plain: A sentence with a typo that makes a different word is missense. A typo that puts a period in the middle of the sentence is nonsense: the sentence stops early.

ox: Wrong. With no lactose, the repressor stays bound to the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. High glucose also keeps cAMP low. Transcription is off.
Wrong. Lactose releases the repressor, but glucose keeps cAMP low, so CAP is not activated. You get only low-level transcription. Trap: thinking lactose alone is enough.

Correct. Lactose becomes allolactose, which binds the repressor and releases it from the operator. Low glucose raises cAMP, which binds CAP and helps RNA polymerase bind. Both signals together give maximum transcription.
Wrong. With no lactose, the repressor stays on the operator. Low glucose would make CAP active, but the gene is still blocked.

p: The lac operon holds genes to digest lactose. It has two controls. A repressor protein blocks the gene unless lactose (as allolactose) is present. That is negative control.

CAP is an activator. It works only when cAMP is high, which happens when glucose is low. That is positive control. Bacteria prefer glucose, so they switch on lactose genes fully only when lactose is present and glucose is gone.

mem: Lactose present: repressor off the operator
Glucose low: cAMP high: CAP active
Max expression needs lactose present AND glucose absent
q10.trap: Stopping once the repressor is released. You also need CAP activation, which needs low glucose.
q10.plain: A light turns on only if two switches are both on: 'there is food I can use' and 'my favorite food is gone'.

ox: Wrong. In anaphase II, sister chromatids separate, but the cells were already haploid (n) after meiosis I. Ploidy stays n. This step looks like mitosis. Trap: confusing it with the halving step.
Wrong. S phase copies DNA, so each chromosome has two chromatids. This increases DNA content but does not change the chromosome count.
Wrong. Crossing over swaps pieces of DNA between homologs. This increases genetic variety but does not reduce the number of chromosomes.
Correct. In anaphase I, each homolog (still two chromatids) moves to an opposite pole. Each daughter cell gets only one chromosome of each pair, so 2n becomes n.

concept.t: What halves chromosome number in meiosis
p: A diploid (2n) cell has two copies of each chromosome, called homologs, one from each parent. Meiosis I separates these homologs into different cells. After that, each cell has just one of each pair, so it is haploid (n).
Meiosis II then separates sister chromatids (the two identical copies of one chromosome). That does not change the chromosome number.

mem: Meiosis I is reductional: homologs separate, 2n to n
Meiosis II is equational: sister chromatids separate
Crossing over happens in prophase I
d_1C_1.trap: Choosing sister chromatid separation because it is the 'separation' you know from mitosis.
d_1C_1.plain: You have two matching shoes in each pair. Meiosis I gives each of two kids one shoe from each pair. Meiosis II just splits each shoe into its two halves.

fig.cap: Meiosis I separates homologs and halves the chromosome number; meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

ox: Correct. In meiosis I, both homologs of the pair go to the same pole. Both daughter cells are abnormal (one has an extra chromosome, one is missing one). Meiosis II then splits each into two, so all four gametes are abnormal: two n+1 and two n-1.
Wrong. Two normal and two abnormal gametes is the result of nondisjunction in meiosis II, where only one of the two cells is affected. The trap is mixing up which division failed.
Wrong. Four normal gametes needs no error. The question says one pair failed to separate.
Wrong. This leaves out the n-1 gametes. The cell that did not receive the pair is missing a chromosome, so n-1 gametes must form. Two n+1 and two normal would not add up.

concept.t: Nondisjunction in meiosis I vs II
p: Nondisjunction means chromosomes fail to separate. In meiosis I, homologous pairs should split apart. If one pair stays together, one cell gets both and the other cell gets none of that chromosome.
Meiosis II then splits sister chromatids in each cell. Both cells were already wrong, so all four gametes are wrong: two with one extra (n+1) and two with one missing (n-1).

mem: Meiosis I error: all 4 gametes abnormal (2 n+1, 2 n-1).
Meiosis II error: 2 normal, 1 n+1, 1 n-1.
Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
d_1C_3.trap: Students mix up meiosis I and II. Remember: error in meiosis I ruins all four gametes.
d_1C_3.plain: Picture two kids who must each take one of a pair of twins home. If one kid takes both twins, the other gets none. Splitting the twins later cannot fix it.

ox: Correct. A few birds start a new population. They carry only a small sample of the mainland gene pool, so a rare allele can become common just by chance. This is the founder effect.
Wrong. Gene flow is ongoing movement of alleles between populations by migrants. One colonization event is not continued exchange. The trap is seeing birds move and saying gene flow.
Wrong. Directional selection needs the allele to give a survival or reproductive advantage. The question gives no such advantage, so chance is the cause.

Wrong. A bottleneck is a sudden crash of an existing population from a disaster. Here, a small group starts a new population in a new place. Both involve few individuals, which is why they are confused.

p: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies, strongest in small groups. The founder effect is drift that happens when a few individuals leave and start a new population.
These founders carry only part of the original gene pool. A rare allele may be missing or overrepresented. Its frequency shifts by chance, not because it helps survival.

mem: Founder effect = new colony started by few individuals.
Bottleneck = existing population shrinks suddenly (disaster).
Both are types of genetic drift: random, not adaptive.
d_1C_8.trap: Founder effect (new place, few colonists) versus bottleneck (same place, population crash).
d_1C_8.plain: If you grab a handful of mixed candy from a big jar, your handful may have lots of a rare flavor just by luck.

ox: Wrong. Completely linked genes never recombine, which means 0 percent recombination. At 50 cM, recombination is at the maximum.
Correct. A recombination frequency of 50 percent matches the result of independent assortment. So genes 50 cM apart, or farther, behave as if unlinked.
Wrong. Recombination frequency cannot exceed 50 percent because multiple crossovers cancel each other out. Trap: thinking 100 percent is possible.
Wrong. No crossovers would mean complete linkage with 0 percent recombination, the opposite of 50 cM.

p: Genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together because they are physically linked. Crossing over can break up the linkage. A centimorgan (cM) is a unit of distance: 1 cM is about 1 percent recombination.

If two genes are far enough apart, crossovers happen so often that half the offspring are recombinant and half are parental. That is exactly what independent assortment gives, so 50 percent is the maximum.

mem: 1 cM is about 1 percent recombination
Maximum recombination frequency is 50 percent
50 percent means unlinked
Closer genes mean lower recombination
d_1C_11.trap: Believing recombination can reach 100 percent or that 50 cM means completely linked.
d_1C_11.plain: Flip a coin for each gene: heads means it is passed from grandma, tails from grandpa. Far-apart genes act like two separate coin flips.

fig.cap: Observed recombination frequency rises with map distance but levels off at 50%, the value for unlinked genes. It can never exceed one half.
fig.alt: Curve of observed recombination frequency against true map distance approaching 50%.

ox: Wrong. Variable expressivity means people who all show the trait have different severity. The first person shows no signs at all, which is a question of whether, not how much.
Wrong. Codominance means both alleles of a gene are fully expressed in a heterozygote, as in AB blood type. It does not explain a missing phenotype.
Wrong. Epistasis is when one gene masks the effect of a different gene. The question does not describe a second gene.
Correct. Penetrance is the percent of people with the genotype who show any phenotype. A carrier with no signs shows incomplete (reduced) penetrance.

p: Penetrance asks: does the person show the trait at all? If only 80 percent of people with the allele show signs, penetrance is 80 percent. That is incomplete penetrance.
Expressivity asks: among people who show the trait, how strong is it? Mild versus severe is variable expressivity.

mem: Penetrance: whether the trait appears (yes or no)
Expressivity: how severe it is when it appears
Incomplete penetrance: carrier with no phenotype

r: Does the carrier show the trait at all?

d_1C_15.trap: Mixing up penetrance (whether) and expressivity (how much).
d_1C_15.plain: Penetrance is whether the light turns on. Expressivity is how bright it shines.

ox: Wrong. Hexokinase is the first step and traps glucose in the cell as G6P, but G6P can still go to glycogen or the pentose phosphate pathway. It is not the committed step.
Correct. PFK-1 turns fructose-6-phosphate into fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. After this step the sugar is committed to glycolysis. It is slowed by ATP and sped up by AMP and F2,6BP.
Wrong. Pyruvate kinase is regulated, but it is the last step, after the commitment has already been made.
Wrong. This enzyme starts the pentose phosphate pathway, a different route. Do not confuse it with glycolysis.

p: Glycolysis breaks glucose into pyruvate. The committed step is the one after which the molecule has no other option but to continue down the pathway. It is usually also the slowest, regulated step.
In glycolysis this is PFK-1. ATP signals the cell has enough energy and turns it down. AMP signals low energy and turns it up.

mem: PFK-1: F6P to F1,6BP is the committed, rate-limiting step.
ATP and citrate inhibit PFK-1; AMP and F2,6BP activate it.
Hexokinase = first step; pyruvate kinase = last step.
q14.trap: Choosing hexokinase because it is first. First is not the same as committed.
q14.plain: Think of a one-way toll gate on a highway. Once your car goes through, you cannot take any exit but the one ahead.

ox: Correct. Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but spends 2 early on, so the net is 2 ATP. It also makes 2 NADH.
Wrong. 4 ATP is the gross yield. You must subtract the 2 ATP invested in the first steps.
Wrong. About 30-32 ATP is the total from complete aerobic breakdown (glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, TCA cycle, electron transport chain).
Wrong. Glycolysis makes NADH. FADH₂ is made in the TCA cycle and in fatty acid oxidation.

p: Glycolysis splits one glucose into two pyruvate. Early steps spend 2 ATP to prepare the sugar. Later steps make 4 ATP.
Net means what is left after paying the cost. It also makes 2 NADH, an electron carrier that can later be used to make more ATP.

mem: Glycolysis net: 2 ATP, 2 NADH, 2 pyruvate.
Gross ATP = 4; invested = 2.
Aerobic total is about 30-32 ATP.

fm.f: Net ATP = ATP made - ATP spent
fm.why: Net yield means profit after the investment.

q15.trap: Reporting the gross 4 ATP instead of the net 2 ATP.
q15.plain: You pay 2 dollars to enter a game and win 4 dollars. You walked away with 2 dollars of profit.

ox: Wrong. Complex I is blocked by rotenone, not cyanide.
Correct. Cyanide binds the iron in complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), so electrons cannot pass to O₂. The whole chain backs up and O₂ use stops.
Wrong. ATP synthase is blocked by oligomycin. That would stop ATP making but the chain problem is different.
Wrong. Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) is inhibited by malonate, not cyanide.

p: The electron transport chain is a line of protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Electrons are passed down the line and finally given to oxygen at complex IV, forming water.
If complex IV is blocked, electrons cannot leave the chain. Everything upstream backs up and oxygen is no longer used.

mem: Cyanide (and CO, azide) block complex IV.
Rotenone blocks complex I; malonate blocks complex II.
Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase.
q16.trap: Mixing up which poison blocks which complex. Oxygen is the final acceptor, so the O₂-related poison hits complex IV.
q16.plain: It is like a bucket line passing water to the end person. If the last person is stuck, the whole line stops.

ox: Correct. A proton leak is an uncoupler. The gradient cannot build, so the chain runs faster to try to fix it and uses more O₂. ATP synthase has little gradient to use, so ATP falls. The energy is lost as heat.
Wrong. Falling O₂ use fits an electron transport chain inhibitor such as cyanide. A leak makes the chain work harder, not slower.
Wrong. ATP synthesis needs the proton gradient. If protons leak back, there is less drive to make ATP.
Wrong. Glycolysis makes only 2 net ATP and cannot make up the loss. Also, the ETC and gradient are directly affected.

p: The electron transport chain pumps protons out of the matrix to build a gradient. Protons flow back through ATP synthase, which makes ATP. This links (couples) O₂ use to ATP making.
An uncoupler lets protons leak back in without passing through ATP synthase. The chain speeds up, O₂ use rises, ATP falls, and the extra energy becomes heat.

mem: Uncoupler: O₂ use up, ATP down, heat up.
Examples: DNP, thermogenin (UCP1) in brown fat.
Inhibitors of the ETC lower O₂ use.
q17.trap: Thinking less ATP always means less O₂ use. Uncouplers speed up O₂ use.
q17.plain: Picture a water wheel with a hole in the pool above. The pump works nonstop to refill the pool, but the wheel barely turns.

ox: Wrong. CoA attaches to the fatty acid in the cytosol but the acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner membrane by itself.
Correct. Carnitine swaps places with CoA, carries the acyl group across, and CoA is reattached in the matrix, where β-oxidation occurs.
Wrong. Albumin carries free fatty acids through the blood, not across the mitochondrial membrane.
Wrong. Chylomicrons carry dietary fat from the gut through lymph and blood.

p: β-oxidation, the breakdown of fatty acids for energy, happens inside the mitochondrial matrix. Long fatty acids must get past the inner mitochondrial membrane, which blocks them.
Carnitine acts as a ferry. It picks up the acyl group, carries it across, and drops it off inside the matrix.

mem: Carnitine carries long-chain acyl groups into the matrix.
CPT-I is the rate-limiting step; malonyl-CoA inhibits it.
Albumin = blood transport; chylomicron = dietary fat transport.
q18.trap: Picking CoA because it is attached to the fatty acid. It activates it but cannot cross.
q18.plain: Carnitine is like a ferry that carries cars across a river where no bridge exists.

fig.cap: Long-chain fatty acids need the carnitine shuttle (CPT-I, translocase, CPT-II) to reach the matrix; short- and medium-chain fatty acids cross without carnitine.
fig.alt: Mitochondrial membranes with long-chain fatty acids blocked without carnitine and medium-chain fatty acids crossing freely.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: A cis double bond kinks the tail, so lipids pack loosely and the membrane stays fluid; saturated and trans tails pack tightly.
fig.alt: Stearic, oleic and elaidic acid chains compared for packing.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: Gap junctions (connexons) join the cytoplasm of neighboring cells so ions and small dyes can pass; the other junctions seal or anchor.
fig.alt: Two epithelial cells with tight, adherens, desmosome, gap junction and hemidesmosome labeled.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. SGLT pulls glucose in using the Na⁺ gradient made by the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase. Without the pump, the gradient fades and glucose uptake falls.
Wrong. Blocking the pump does not give more useful Na⁺. The Na⁺ gradient collapses, and the gradient is what drives SGLT.
Wrong. SGLT does not use ATP directly. It is secondary active transport, using the Na⁺ gradient that ATP built.
Wrong. Glucose does not flow in reverse. The transporter simply loses its driving force and slows down.

p: Primary active transport uses ATP directly. The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pumps Na⁺ out of the cell, creating a low-Na⁺ inside.
Secondary active transport uses that stored gradient. SGLT lets Na⁺ flow in, and glucose comes along. If the pump is blocked, the gradient is lost and so is the glucose uptake.

mem: Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase = primary active transport; it sets the gradient.
SGLT = secondary active, symport of Na⁺ and glucose.
Ouabain and digoxin inhibit the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase.
d_2A_3.trap: Believing a cotransporter uses ATP itself. It uses the gradient made by an ATP pump.
d_2A_3.plain: A water slide only works if someone keeps carrying water up the hill. Stop the carrying and the slide stops.

fig.cap: SGLT1 uses the Na⁺ gradient made by the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Ouabain stops the pump, the gradient runs down, and glucose uptake falls.
fig.alt: Intestinal cell with apical SGLT1, basolateral GLUT2 and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. The protein is made on the rough ER, sent to the Golgi for processing, packed into secretory vesicles, and released by exocytosis at the plasma membrane.
Wrong. This puts the Golgi before the rough ER. Also, lysosomes digest material and are not on the secretion route.
Wrong. The nucleus holds DNA but does not make secreted proteins. The route also ends in a lysosome, not at the cell surface.
Wrong. Smooth ER makes lipids, not secreted proteins. Peroxisomes handle oxidative reactions and are not on this route.

p: Proteins to be exported are built by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum (ER), which is studded with ribosomes. They enter the ER space as they are made.
Vesicles (small membrane bubbles) carry them to the Golgi, which modifies and sorts them. Secretory vesicles then fuse with the plasma membrane and release them outside (exocytosis).

mem: Order: rough ER, Golgi, vesicle, plasma membrane.
Rough ER makes secreted and membrane proteins.
Lysosome is a different destination from secretion.
d_2A_10.trap: Reversing the order of the ER and Golgi, or sending the protein to a lysosome.
d_2A_10.plain: It is like a factory line: build the product, wrap and label it, load it on a truck, and deliver it out the front door.

fig.cap: Secreted proteins go rough ER → cis Golgi → medial → trans Golgi → vesicles to the cell surface.
fig.alt: ER, Golgi cisternae from cis to trans, and the three exit routes.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Wrong. Stratified squamous has many layers and protects, like skin. Gas would diffuse too slowly through it.
Wrong. This lines the larger airways and uses cilia to sweep mucus. It is too thick for gas exchange.
Correct. One thin layer of flat cells gives the shortest diffusion distance, so gases pass quickly between air and blood.
Wrong. Columnar cells are tall, built for absorption and secretion. The extra thickness slows diffusion.

p: Epithelium is tissue that covers surfaces. Simple means one layer; stratified means many layers. Squamous means flat; columnar means tall.
Gas moves by diffusion, which is faster over a short distance. A single layer of flat cells is the thinnest option, so it fits the alveoli and capillary walls.

mem: Simple squamous: diffusion (alveoli, capillaries).
Stratified squamous: protection (skin).
Simple columnar: absorption (gut); ciliated pseudostratified: airways.
d_2A_17.trap: Choosing the tougher, protective epithelium. Exchange needs thin, not tough.
d_2A_17.plain: Passing a note through a thin sheet of paper is easy. Passing it through a thick book is not.

fig.cap: Simple squamous epithelium is one flat layer, giving the thinnest barrier and the fastest diffusion (Fick's law).
fig.alt: Alveolar simple squamous barrier compared with a thick stratified layer.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Wrong. This is the older Davson-Danielli model, with protein sheets on both sides of lipid. Later evidence showed proteins are embedded in the bilayer.
Wrong. Flip-flop of phospholipids between leaflets is slow because the polar head must pass through the oily core. It needs flippase enzymes. Lateral movement is the fast kind.
Wrong. The bilayer is fluid, not a rigid lattice. Many proteins drift sideways, as experiments such as FRAP show.
Correct. The membrane is a 2D fluid. Lipids and many proteins slide sideways in their own leaflet, and proteins are scattered like a mosaic.

p: A plasma membrane is a bilayer: two layers of phospholipids with water-loving heads outside and oily tails inside. Proteins are embedded in it or attached to it.
Fluid means the parts can move sideways. Mosaic means proteins are scattered in a pattern, like tiles. Moving from one layer to the other is rare and slow.

mem: Lateral diffusion is fast; flip-flop is slow without flippase.
Proteins can be integral (embedded) or peripheral (attached).
Fluid mosaic replaced the protein-sandwich model.
x2A_001.trap: Believing lipids flip easily between leaflets, or that proteins are fixed in place.
x2A_001.plain: Think of a crowded dance floor where people slide around freely, but no one can easily jump to the floor above.

fig.cap: A section of plasma membrane: integral and peripheral proteins sit in a fluid bilayer where lateral diffusion is fast and flip-flop is slow. Below, the current model is compared with the abandoned protein-sandwich model.
fig.alt: Schematic bilayer of phospholipids with a single-pass and a multipass integral protein, a glycan, and a peripheral protein on the cytosolic face; a green double arrow labelled lateral diffusion fast; a red arrow across the bilayer labelled flip-flop slow. Lower panels contrast the fluid mosaic model with the Davson-Danielli protein-lipid-protein sandwich.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Wrong. This is the effect of cholesterol at high temperature, where it restrains tail motion. In the cold, it does the opposite.
Wrong. Cholesterol lowers permeability to ions and small polar molecules because it fills gaps between lipids.
Wrong. Cholesterol is not an enzyme. Flippases catalyze lipid flip-flop.
Correct. Cholesterol's rigid ring wedges between the fatty acid tails so they cannot pack tightly into a gel, which keeps the membrane fluid in the cold.

p: Membrane fluidity changes with temperature. In the cold, lipid tails pack tightly and the membrane stiffens. When warm, the tails move more and the membrane becomes loose.
Cholesterol sits between the tails. In the cold it blocks tight packing, raising fluidity. In the heat it limits tail motion, lowering fluidity.

mem: Cholesterol is a fluidity buffer.
Cold: prevents packing, so more fluid. Hot: restrains motion, so less fluid.
Unsaturated tails also raise fluidity; longer, saturated tails lower it.
x2A_002.trap: Saying cholesterol always makes membranes more rigid. It depends on temperature.
x2A_002.plain: Cholesterol is like putting a few pencils between stacked papers. In the cold it stops them from stacking flat. When things get wild, it keeps them from sliding all over.

fig.cap: Illustrative model curves of fluidity versus temperature. Without cholesterol the bilayer melts sharply from gel to fluid; with cholesterol the change is gentler, so the membrane is more fluid in the cold and less fluid when warm.
fig.alt: Graph of membrane fluidity versus temperature from 0 to 50 degrees Celsius. A blue curve without cholesterol rises steeply around 25 degrees from low to high fluidity. An orange curve with cholesterol rises gradually, sitting above the blue curve in the cold region and below it in the warm region.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph from illustrative logistic curves; it shows the well-established qualitative effect, not measured data.

fig.cap: Gram-negative bacteria have an outer membrane outside a thin peptidoglycan layer, an extra barrier that keeps many large or hydrophobic agents out. Gram-positives have a thick wall and no outer membrane.
fig.alt: Gram-positive and Gram-negative cell envelopes side by side.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: Wall-synthesis inhibitors such as penicillin kill only cells that are building new wall, so growing cells lyse and non-growing cells survive.
fig.alt: Viable count over time with penicillin added in exponential versus stationary phase.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from code. Illustrative.

fig.cap: A batch culture shows lag (cells adjust, little division), exponential growth, stationary phase (nutrient limits growth) and death.
fig.alt: Log viable count against time with lag, exponential, stationary and death phases.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from code. Illustrative model.

fig.cap: Oxygen diffuses only about 0.1 to 0.2 mm, so a tumor beyond 1 to 2 mm stalls (with death balancing division) until VEGF recruits new vessels.
fig.alt: Tumor with a hypoxic core secreting VEGF, new vessel sprouts, and an anti-VEGF antibody.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall on the outside and no outer membrane. The thick wall traps the crystal violet dye, so they stain purple.
Wrong. This is Gram-negative bacteria, which have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane holding LPS (lipopolysaccharide). Trap: mixing up the two groups.
Wrong. Almost all bacteria have a wall. Mycoplasma is the famous exception. Trap: choosing the exception instead of the rule.
Wrong. Gram-negative cells stain pink or red because the thin wall loses the purple dye. Trap: remembering pink and linking it to the wrong group.

p: The Gram stain sorts bacteria by their cell wall. Peptidoglycan is a mesh of sugars and amino acids that gives the wall strength.
Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan, no outer membrane, stains purple. Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan, plus an outer membrane with LPS, stains pink.

mem: Gram-positive = thick wall, purple, no outer membrane.
Gram-negative = thin wall, pink, outer membrane with LPS.
Mycoplasma has no cell wall.
q23.trap: Swapping the colors. Positive keeps the purple stain; negative loses it and shows pink.
q23.plain: A thick winter coat holds the dye in like a sponge. A thin jacket lets it wash out.

ox: Wrong. Transformation is when a bacterium picks up free, naked DNA from its surroundings. No virus is involved. Trap: both move DNA, so they sound alike.
Correct. In transduction, a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria) carries bacterial DNA from one cell to another. The virus is the vector.
Wrong. Conjugation moves DNA directly between two bacteria through a sex pilus (a tube-like bridge). No virus needed.
Wrong. Binary fission is how a bacterium divides into two copies. It does not transfer DNA between different cells.

p: Bacteria share genes in three ways. Each has a different carrier.
Transformation: free DNA from the environment. Transduction: a bacteriophage carries the DNA. Conjugation: a direct bridge (sex pilus) between two cells.

mem: Transformation = naked DNA taken up.
Transduction = virus (phage) carries DNA.
Conjugation = pilus contact between cells.
Binary fission = reproduction, not gene transfer.
q24.mn: Transduction has the word 'duct' like a delivery tube: a virus delivers the DNA.
q24.trap: Mixing up transformation and transduction. Look for the word 'bacteriophage' or 'virus' to pick transduction.
q24.plain: Transduction is like a mail carrier (the virus) delivering a package (DNA) from one house to another.

ox: Correct. Reverse transcriptase is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase. It reads the viral RNA and builds a DNA copy.
Wrong. Integrase inserts the finished DNA copy into the host genome. It comes after the copy is made. Trap: both enzymes are retrovirus steps.
Wrong. RNA replicase copies RNA into RNA, which is used by some other RNA viruses. A retrovirus needs RNA to DNA.
Wrong. DNA polymerase I in bacteria removes RNA primers and fills gaps. It reads a DNA template, not an RNA genome.

p: A retrovirus (like HIV) stores its genes as RNA. The host cell reads DNA, so the virus needs to convert its RNA to DNA first.
Reverse transcriptase does this conversion. Then integrase puts the DNA into the host chromosome, where it is copied as a normal gene.

mem: Reverse transcriptase: RNA to DNA.
Integrase: inserts viral DNA into the host genome.
Retroviruses go RNA to DNA to RNA to protein.
q25.trap: Choosing integrase. It joins DNA into the genome but does not make the DNA from RNA.
q25.plain: It is like translating a message from a foreign language into the language the town speaks, so the locals can use it.

fig.cap: DNA damage stabilizes p53, which turns on p21. p21 blocks the cyclin–CDKs that phosphorylate Rb, so E2F stays bound and the cell pauses in G1.
fig.alt: Pathway from DNA damage through p53 and p21 to blocked cyclin–CDK and Rb–E2F.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: p53 is kept low by constant destruction; DNA damage stabilizes it. It then arrests the cycle (p21) or triggers apoptosis (Bax, PUMA). Cells without p53 keep dividing with damage.
fig.alt: Flowchart from DNA damage to p53 and its two outcomes.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: p53 is kept low by constant destruction; DNA damage stabilizes it. It then arrests the cycle (p21) or triggers apoptosis (Bax, PUMA). Cells without p53 keep dividing with damage.
fig.alt: Flowchart from DNA damage to p53 and its two outcomes.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: An unattached kinetochore keeps the spindle checkpoint on: APC/C stays inhibited, cohesin is not cut, and the cell is held in mitosis.
fig.alt: Spindle assembly checkpoint from an unattached kinetochore to cohesin cleavage.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

fig.cap: Apoptosis is orderly: the cell shrinks into membrane-wrapped bodies that are engulfed without spilling contents. Necrosis swells and bursts, causing inflammation.
fig.alt: Apoptosis and necrosis compared step by step.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram, drawn from code.

ox: Correct. p53 is a tumor suppressor. After DNA damage it stops the cell at the G1/S checkpoint so repair can happen. If damage is too bad, it triggers apoptosis (programmed cell death).
Wrong. Oncogenes push the cell to divide. p53 does the opposite. Trap: confusing tumor suppressors with oncogenes.
Wrong. Cyclins rise and fall with the cell cycle. p53 is a transcription factor that turns genes on or off, not a cyclin.
Wrong. Telomerase lengthens telomeres (chromosome ends). It is not related to p53's role.

concept.t: p53, the guardian of the genome
p: p53 is a protein that checks for DNA damage. It is a tumor suppressor: a gene whose job is to stop uncontrolled growth.
When DNA is damaged, p53 turns on genes (like p21) that pause the cycle at G1/S. If repair fails, p53 pushes the cell into apoptosis.

mem: p53 = tumor suppressor; loss of p53 helps cancer grow.
It arrests the cell at G1/S or triggers apoptosis.
Oncogenes speed division; tumor suppressors brake it.
q26.trap: Calling p53 an oncogene. Loss of a tumor suppressor causes cancer; gain of an oncogene does.
q26.plain: p53 is a safety inspector who stops the factory line when something is broken, and shuts down the machine if it cannot be fixed.

ox: Correct. Ectoderm is the outer germ layer. It forms the epidermis (skin) and the nervous system.
Wrong. Heart and kidneys come from mesoderm, the middle layer. Trap: thinking of organs in general as outer structures.
Wrong. Gut lining and lungs come from endoderm, the inner layer.
Wrong. Bone and skeletal muscle come from mesoderm.

p: Early embryos have three layers of cells. Each becomes different body parts.
Ectoderm (outer): skin and nervous system. Mesoderm (middle): muscle, bone, heart, kidneys, blood. Endoderm (inner): gut lining, lungs, liver, pancreas.

mem: Ectoderm = skin (epidermis) + nervous system.
Mesoderm = muscle, bone, heart, kidney, blood.
Endoderm = gut lining, lungs, liver, pancreas.
q27.trap: Mixing up mesoderm and endoderm for organs such as kidneys and lungs.
q27.sc: Ecto = outer, like exterior: the outer layer makes the outer covering (skin) and the nervous system. Endo = inner, like the gut lining.
q27.plain: Think of a three-layer cake. The top layer becomes the skin and the brain, the middle becomes muscles and bones, the bottom becomes the insides of tubes like the gut.

ox: Wrong. In prophase, chromatin condenses into chromosomes and the spindle begins to form. The chromatids are still joined.
Wrong. In metaphase, chromosomes line up at the middle plate. They are still paired. Trap: this is just before the separation.
Correct. In anaphase, cohesin (the protein glue holding sister chromatids) is cleaved. The chromatids are pulled to opposite poles.
Wrong. In telophase, nuclear envelopes re-form around the separated sets. Separation already happened.

p: A sister chromatid is one of two identical copies of a chromosome, joined at the centromere. Mitosis splits them so each new cell gets one copy.
The order is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. Splitting happens in anaphase.

mem: Prophase: condense. Metaphase: line up. Anaphase: apart. Telophase: two nuclei.
Anaphase = sister chromatids separate (mitosis).
In meiosis I, homologs separate; in meiosis II, sister chromatids separate.
q28.mn: PMAT: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase. 'A' for Apart.
q28.trap: Picking metaphase because it is the famous lineup stage. Separation comes right after it.
q28.plain: Two kids holding hands line up in the middle of the room (metaphase). In anaphase someone lets go and each kid walks to opposite sides.

ox: Correct. High CO₂, high H⁺ (lower pH) in active muscle lowers Hb's affinity for O₂ (Bohr effect), so the curve shifts right and more O₂ is released.
Wrong. Cooler temperature increases affinity and shifts the curve left. Trap: forgetting heat shifts right.
Wrong. Fetal Hb binds O₂ more tightly than adult Hb, shifting the curve left so it can take O₂ from mom. Trap: thinking fetal Hb unloads easily.
Wrong. CO binds Hb strongly and also makes remaining O₂ bind more tightly, shifting left. Trap: assuming a poison lowers affinity.

p: The oxyhemoglobin curve shows how full Hb is with O₂ at different O₂ pressures. A right shift means Hb lets go of O₂ more easily (lower affinity). A left shift means Hb holds O₂ tighter.
Right shift: more CO₂, more H⁺ (lower pH), higher temperature, more 2,3-BPG. These happen in working muscle, which needs more O₂.

mem: Right shift: high CO₂, H⁺, temperature, 2,3-BPG
Left shift: opposites, plus fetal Hb and CO
Right shift = lower affinity = more unloading
q34.mn: CADET face Right: CO₂, Acid, 2,3-BPG (DPG), Exercise, Temperature all shift the curve right.
q34.trap: Mixing up which direction means higher affinity. Right = release.
q34.plain: Hot, busy muscles call out for oxygen, so the delivery truck drops off its cargo more easily.

ox: Correct. Aldosterone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct to keep Na⁺ and excrete K⁺. Water follows Na⁺, raising blood volume.
Wrong. Inserting aquaporins to reabsorb water is ADH. Trap: mixing up the two hormones.
Wrong. Decreasing Na⁺ reabsorption is ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide). Aldosterone does the opposite. Trap: reversing the direction.
Wrong. Glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, mostly by transporters, not by aldosterone. Trap: picking the wrong segment.

p: Aldosterone is a steroid hormone from the adrenal cortex. It acts in the distal tubule and collecting duct. It makes cells reabsorb sodium (Na⁺) and secrete potassium (K⁺).
Water follows sodium by osmosis, so blood volume and pressure rise. The renin-angiotensin system triggers aldosterone release when pressure is low.

mem: Aldosterone: Na⁺ in, K⁺ out, water follows
ADH: water only, via aquaporins
ANP: opposite of aldosterone
q35.plain: Aldosterone is a salt-saver. It tells the kidney to keep salt and water in the body.

ox: Wrong. Pepsin is the stomach protease, made from pepsinogen. It does not activate trypsinogen. Trap: choosing the most famous protease.
Correct. Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) on the duodenal lining cuts trypsinogen into active trypsin. Trypsin then activates other pancreatic zymogens.
Wrong. HCl activates pepsinogen to pepsin in the stomach, not trypsinogen. Trap: mixing up the two activations.
Wrong. Bile salts emulsify fats, breaking large drops into small ones. They do not cut proteins. Trap: confusing digestive helpers.

p: Pancreatic enzymes are made as inactive precursors called zymogens, so they do not digest the pancreas itself. Trypsinogen is one.
In the duodenum (first part of the small intestine), enteropeptidase cuts trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin then activates more trypsinogen and other zymogens (chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase).

mem: Enteropeptidase: trypsinogen to trypsin
Trypsin activates the other zymogens
HCl activates pepsinogen in the stomach
q36.trap: Choosing pepsin or HCl because they are the stomach's famous activators.
q36.plain: A safety cap keeps a tool locked. A key in the intestine unlocks the first tool, and that tool unlocks the rest.

ox: Wrong. Helper T cells release cytokines that direct B cells and others, but they do not make antibodies. Trap: confusing coordinating with producing.
Correct. Plasma cells are activated B cells that make and secrete large amounts of antibodies.
Wrong. Macrophages eat pathogens and show antigens to T cells. They do not secrete antibodies. Trap: assuming all immune cells do all jobs.
Wrong. NK cells kill infected or tumor cells directly, without antibodies. Trap: mixing innate and adaptive cells.

p: B cells are white blood cells of the adaptive immune system. When a B cell meets its antigen (a molecule it recognizes), often with help from helper T cells, it becomes a plasma cell.
Plasma cells are antibody factories. Antibodies are proteins that bind specific antigens. Some B cells become memory B cells for future infections.

mem: Plasma cell = secreting B cell
Helper T (CD4) = coordinate
Cytotoxic T (CD8) and NK = kill cells directly
q37.trap: Picking helper T cells because they are called the 'conductors' of the response.
q37.plain: A B cell is a recruit who learns the enemy's face. A plasma cell is the factory that mass-produces wanted posters for that face.

ox: Wrong. The stomach mostly churns and starts digesting protein. Only alcohol and a few drugs cross its wall well. Trap: thinking digestion and absorption happen in the same place.
Correct. The small intestine is lined with folds, villi and tiny microvilli, which create a huge surface area. Sugars, amino acids, fats, vitamins and minerals are absorbed here.
Wrong. The large intestine mainly takes back water and electrolytes and holds waste. Trap: picking the 'last stop' because it feels like the final step.
Wrong. The esophagus is only a tube that moves food by peristalsis (wave-like squeezing). Nothing is absorbed there.

p: Digestion means breaking food into small pieces. Absorption means moving those pieces into the blood or lymph. Most absorption happens in the small intestine.
Its wall has villi (finger-like folds) covered in microvilli (tiny hairs on each cell). These make a very large surface area, so nutrients pass into the body quickly.

mem: Small intestine = main site of nutrient absorption
Villi and microvilli = more surface area
Large intestine = water and electrolytes
Stomach absorbs almost nothing (alcohol, some drugs)
q38.trap: Do not confuse where digestion starts (mouth, stomach) with where absorption mostly happens (small intestine).
q38.plain: A paper towel with lots of folds soaks up more water than a flat sheet. The villi are the folds.

ox: Correct. Average velocity = displacement / time. After one full lap she is back at the start, so displacement is 0 and average velocity is 0.
Wrong. 5 m/s is average speed (400 m / 80 s), which uses total distance. Trap: mixing up speed and velocity.
Wrong. 10 m/s has no basis here; it comes from using a wrong time or doubling. Trap: guessing from the numbers.
Wrong. 400 m/s is just the distance with no division by time. Trap: forgetting to divide.

p: Distance is the total path length. Displacement is the straight-line change in position from start to end, with direction.
Velocity uses displacement. Speed uses distance. If you end where you started, displacement is zero, so average velocity is zero.

mem: Average velocity = displacement / time
Average speed = distance / time
Round trip: displacement = 0

fm.f: v_avg = displacement / time, where v_avg = average velocity, displacement = final position minus start position, time = elapsed time
fm.v: displacement = 0 m (back at start), time = 80 s
fm.why: Velocity is defined by displacement, not by distance traveled.
fm.nc: Zero divided by anything is zero.

d_4A_1.trap: The 5 m/s answer is average speed. The question asks for velocity.
d_4A_1.plain: If you walk around the block and end at your front door, you have moved a lot but you are not any closer to where you began.

ox: Wrong. 10 m/s is only the horizontal part. The ball also speeds up downward. Trap: ignoring vertical gain.
Wrong. 20 m/s is only the vertical part after 2 s. The horizontal 10 m/s still counts. Trap: ignoring the horizontal component.
Correct. Horizontal speed stays 10 m/s. Vertical speed = gt = 10 × 2 = 20 m/s. Speed = √(10² + 20²) = √(500), about 22 m/s.
Wrong. 30 m/s adds 10 + 20 directly. Components at right angles must be combined with the Pythagorean theorem. Trap: adding perpendicular vectors like plain numbers.

p: A projectile's horizontal and vertical motions are independent. With no air resistance, horizontal velocity stays constant. Vertical velocity grows by g (acceleration due to gravity) every second.
The total speed is the length of the diagonal made by the two components, found with the Pythagorean theorem.

mem: Horizontal velocity is constant
Vertical velocity = g x t (from rest vertically)
Combine perpendicular components with a² + b² = c²

fm.f: v = √(vx² + vy²), where vx = horizontal speed, vy = vertical speed = g x t, g = 10 m/s², t = time
fm.why: The two components are perpendicular, so use Pythagoras.

d_4A_3.sc: The answer must be bigger than 20 and less than 30 (10 + 20), so only 22 fits.
d_4A_3.trap: Adding perpendicular components arithmetically gives 30, which is too large.
d_4A_3.plain: A ball rolling off a table keeps rolling sideways at the same pace while it also falls faster and faster.

ox: Wrong. Both at half speed keeps momentum, but kinetic energy falls to 1/2 of the original (2 × 1/2 m(v/2)² = 1/4 mv², versus 1/2 mv² at the start), so it is not elastic. Trap: splitting speed evenly.

Correct. With equal masses in a head-on elastic collision, momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved only if the velocities swap. The first ball stops and the second leaves at the original speed.
Wrong. Sticking together is a perfectly inelastic collision, which loses kinetic energy. Trap: applying the inelastic result.
Wrong. If the first ball rebounded while the second moved at the same speed, total momentum would change from mv to 0. Momentum must be conserved.

p: In an elastic collision, both momentum (mass x velocity) and kinetic energy (energy of motion) are conserved. In an inelastic collision, kinetic energy is lost.
When two equal masses collide head-on and elastically, one is at rest, they simply exchange velocities. The mover stops and the resting ball takes off.

mem: Elastic: momentum and KE conserved
Inelastic: only momentum conserved
Equal masses, head-on, elastic: velocities swap
d_4A_18.trap: Do not use the stick-together (inelastic) result for a collision labeled elastic.
d_4A_18.plain: Newton's cradle toy: swing one ball in and exactly one ball swings out on the other side.

ox: Wrong. 80 N over 2 m of rope is what you get with no machine at all. A movable pulley reduces the force needed. Trap: ignoring the pulley.
Wrong. 40 N with only 2 m of rope would be 80 J of work to do 160 J of lifting, which creates energy from nothing. Trap: forgetting that rope length doubles.
Correct. A movable pulley supports the load with two rope segments, so force is halved (40 N) and rope pulled is doubled (4 m). Work = 40 × 4 = 160 J, same as lifting 80 N by 2 m.
Wrong. 160 N and 1 m reverses the trade: it would increase force and cut distance. Trap: flipping the relationship.

p: Work is force times distance moved along the force. A simple machine such as a pulley changes how much force you need, but not the work done (in the ideal, no-friction case).
If a machine cuts the force in half, you must pull twice as far. Force goes down, distance goes up, work stays the same.

mem: Ideal machine: work in = work out
Movable pulley: force halves, rope length doubles
Machines trade force for distance

fm.f: W = F x d, where W = work (J), F = force (N), d = distance (m)
fm.v: Lifting: F = 80 N, d = 2 m. Pulling: F = 40 N, d = 4 m
fm.why: Equal work in and out is the check for an ideal machine.
fm.nc: Multiply whole numbers; 8 × 2 = 16, then add a zero.

d_4A_23.trap: Machines never reduce the work needed; they only trade force for distance.
d_4A_23.plain: Climbing a long gentle ramp is easier than a steep one, but you walk farther.

ox: Wrong. The 30 degree ball does not go farther. Range depends on sin(2 θ); 30 and 60 degrees give the same value. Trap: assuming a flatter throw goes farther.
Correct. Range is proportional to sin(2 θ), and sin 60 = sin 120, so complementary angles (30 and 60) have equal range. Height scales with sin²(θ), so the steeper 60 degree ball rises higher.
Wrong. Ranges are equal, not larger for 60 degrees, and heights are not equal. Trap: thinking a bigger angle means bigger everything.
Wrong. Ranges are equal but the 60 degree ball goes higher, since height depends on sin²(θ). Trap: assuming equal range means equal path.

p: Launch angle θ is measured above the ground. Range (horizontal distance) is proportional to sin(2 θ). Maximum height is proportional to sin²(θ).
Two angles that add up to 90 degrees (complementary) give the same range. The steeper one spends more time in the air and climbs higher.

mem: Range ~ sin(2 θ); max at 45 degrees
Complementary angles = equal range
Height ~ sin²(θ); steeper = higher
d_4A_30.trap: Larger angle does not mean longer range. Range peaks at 45 degrees.
d_4A_30.plain: A basketball lobbed high and one shot on a flatter arc can land in the same spot, but the lob gets higher.

ox: One capillary is narrow, but there are billions in parallel. Velocity depends on the total area they add up to, which is huge, so velocity falls.
Pressure drops steadily from aorta to veins, so it is not constant. And velocity is set by continuity, not by constant pressure.
Capillary resistance is high, but that lowers pressure. Speed is governed by total cross-sectional area, not resistance.
Correct. Continuity says A1 v1 = A2 v2. If total area is 1000 times larger, velocity is about 1000 times lower. Slow flow gives time for exchange.

p: Continuity says that the flow rate (volume per second) is the same all along the circuit: area times velocity is constant. Cross-sectional area is the size of the opening that blood flows through.
Capillaries are tiny, but together they have a far larger total area than the aorta. So blood slows down there, which gives time for oxygen and nutrients to move into tissues.

mem: A x v = constant (flow rate).
Total capillary area is largest, so velocity is lowest.
Aorta has highest velocity; capillaries lowest.

fm.f: A1 x v1 = A2 x v2, where A = total cross-sectional area, v = velocity
fm.why: Blood is incompressible, so flow rate is the same at each level.

d_4B_1.trap: Looking at one capillary's tiny radius instead of the total area of all capillaries in parallel.
d_4B_1.plain: A river squeezed into one narrow channel rushes. When it spreads into a wide marsh, the water barely moves.

ox: Correct. In a narrowed segment the same flow squeezes through a smaller area, so the blood speeds up (continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂). Bernoulli then says that in a horizontal vessel faster flow goes with LOWER pressure.
Incorrect. Faster flow does NOT come with higher pressure. In a horizontal tube, kinetic energy per volume (½ρv²) rises at the expense of pressure.
Incorrect. The narrowing makes blood go FASTER, not slower. Slower flow would happen where the vessel widens.
Incorrect. Pressure is lower, but velocity is not. Both must be considered together: narrow → fast → low pressure.

concept.t: Continuity and Bernoulli in a narrowed vessel
p: The continuity equation says that the volume of fluid passing each point per second is constant: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. A smaller cross-section A means a larger speed v. Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal tube, P + ½ρv² = constant, then says that higher speed means lower pressure.

d_4B_3.trap: Thinking that a narrowing raises pressure because it feels 'squeezed'. Static pressure in the narrow, fast part is actually lower.
mem: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ (narrow → fast).
Bernoulli (horizontal): P + ½ρv² = constant (fast → low pressure).
Narrow = Fast = Low pressure (in a horizontal tube).

fm.f: A₁·v₁ = A₂·v₂, where A = cross-sectional area of the vessel, v = speed of the blood; subscript 1 = normal segment, 2 = narrowed segment
fm.v: Say the narrow segment has half the area: A₂ = ½A₁, and v₁ = 1 (any unit)
fm.s: A₁·1 = ½A₁·v₂ → v₂ = 2. Speed doubles; then P + ½ρv² constant means P drops
fm.why: We use continuity first because it tells us how the speed changes; Bernoulli then converts that speed change into a pressure change.

d_4B_3.sc: Area down → speed up (continuity). Speed up → pressure down (Bernoulli). Two steps, no numbers needed.
d_4B_3.mn: Narrow = Fast = Low: N-F-L, like the 'NFL' of fluids.
d_4B_3.plain: Think of a garden hose: pinch the end and the water shoots out faster. The fast water has less 'push sideways' on the walls, so its pressure is lower.

ox: Correct. Myoglobin has ONE heme and no cooperativity, so its curve is a hyperbola. Its P50 is about 2 mmHg, so it holds O₂ tightly even at very low PO₂ (higher affinity than hemoglobin).
Incorrect. A sigmoidal curve with lower affinity describes HEMOGLOBIN (4 subunits, cooperative, P50 ≈ 26 mmHg), not myoglobin.
Incorrect. Myoglobin does have higher affinity, but a sigmoidal curve requires cooperativity between subunits. Myoglobin has just one, so its curve cannot be sigmoidal.
Incorrect. Hyperbolic is right, but lower affinity is wrong. A P50 of about 2 mmHg is much lower than hemoglobin's 26 mmHg, which means HIGHER affinity.

p: Hemoglobin has four subunits that help each other (cooperativity), giving an S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve with P50 ≈ 26 mmHg. Myoglobin has one subunit, so it simply binds O₂ with a hyperbolic curve and P50 ≈ 2 mmHg. Lower P50 = higher affinity: myoglobin stores O₂ in muscle and releases it only when PO₂ is very low.

d_4B_10.trap: Assuming the sigmoidal curve belongs to the protein with the higher affinity.
mem: Mb: 1 heme, hyperbolic, P50 ≈ 2 mmHg, stores O₂ in muscle.
Hb: 4 hemes, sigmoidal, P50 ≈ 26 mmHg, delivers O₂.
Lower P50 = higher affinity = curve further LEFT.
d_4B_10.sc: Smaller P50 means it grabs O₂ harder, so its curve sits further to the left.
d_4B_10.mn: Mb = Muscle bank (stores O₂). Hb = Hauls and hands off O₂.
d_4B_10.plain: Myoglobin is a warehouse that holds on tight to oxygen; hemoglobin is a delivery truck that drops it off where tissues need it.

ox: Incorrect. Oxygen content does not change how fast a liquid flows through a tube. The question is about fluid flow, which depends on pressure, radius, length and viscosity.
Incorrect. Radius is unchanged, but viscosity is NOT unchanged. More red cells make blood thicker, so flow changes even though radius stays the same.
Correct. Poiseuille: Q = ΔP·πr⁴ / (8ηL). ΔP, r and L stay the same, but η (viscosity) rises with hematocrit, so Q falls. Thicker blood is harder to push.
Incorrect. Density plays no role in Poiseuille flow. Viscosity (resistance to flow), not density (mass per volume), is what rises with more red cells.

p: Poiseuille's law gives the flow rate of a viscous fluid through a tube: Q = ΔP·πr⁴ / (8ηL). Flow rises with pressure difference and with radius to the FOURTH power, and falls with viscosity and length. Blood viscosity rises with hematocrit, which is why polycythemia makes blood harder to move.

d_4B_12.trap: Thinking more red cells means more flow because more oxygen is carried. Flow rate here is fluid mechanics, not oxygen delivery.
mem: Poiseuille: Q = ΔP·πr⁴ / (8ηL).
Flow ∝ r⁴ (a tiny change in radius matters a lot) and ∝ 1/η.
Higher hematocrit → higher viscosity → lower flow.

fm.f: Q = ΔP·π·r⁴ / (8·η·L), where Q = flow rate, ΔP = pressure difference, r = vessel radius, η = viscosity, L = vessel length
fm.v: ΔP, r and L unchanged; η goes UP
fm.s: Q ∝ 1/η, so if η doubles then Q is cut in half
fm.why: We use Poiseuille's law because it tells us how each property of the vessel and the fluid changes flow.

d_4B_12.sc: Change one variable at a time: with pressure and tube fixed, flow moves opposite to viscosity.
d_4B_12.mn: Radius to the Fourth power rules the tube; viscosity is the enemy: thicker = slower.
d_4B_12.plain: Blood with more red cells is like switching from water to syrup: it pours more slowly through the same straw.

ox: Oxygen is carried by blood, bound to hemoglobin. Lymph vessels do not transport oxygen to tissues.
Lymph does not directly raise capillary oncotic pressure (the pull of plasma proteins). Returning protein only helps indirectly.
Correct. Capillaries filter out more fluid than they take back. Lymph collects the extra fluid and leaked protein and returns it to the veins.
Lymphatic vessels start in the tissue spaces (interstitium), not at arterioles.

p: Capillaries leak fluid into tissue spaces (filtration) and take some back (reabsorption). More leaves than returns. The interstitium is the space between cells.
The lymphatic system is a one-way drain. It collects the extra fluid (lymph) and protein and returns them to veins. Without it, tissues swell (edema).

mem: Filtration exceeds reabsorption; lymph returns the surplus.
Lymph also returns protein that leaked out.
Blocked lymph causes edema.
d_4B_17.trap: Forgetting that capillaries filter more than they reabsorb, which is why a drain is needed.
d_4B_17.plain: A sink with a faucet slightly faster than the drain overflows. Lymph vessels are an extra drain that keeps the floor dry.

ox: Wrong. This swaps the electrodes. Oxidation never happens at the cathode, and electrons do not flow from cathode to anode.
Wrong. Reduction happens at the cathode, not the anode. The direction anode to cathode is right but the label is wrong.
Wrong. Reduction at the cathode is right, but electrons flow from anode to cathode. The direction is reversed.
Correct. Oxidation at the anode frees electrons. They travel through the wire to the cathode, where a species is reduced.

p: A galvanic cell uses a spontaneous redox reaction to make electricity. Oxidation (losing electrons) happens at the anode. Reduction (gaining electrons) happens at the cathode.
Electrons always move from the anode to the cathode through the wire.

mem: Oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode (always)
Electrons flow anode to cathode
In a galvanic cell, the anode is negative and the cathode is positive
d_4C_1.mn: An Ox and Red Cat: Anode = Oxidation, Reduction = Cathode. Also, LEO the lion says GER: Lose Electrons Oxidation, Gain Electrons Reduction.
d_4C_1.trap: Mixing up electron flow with conventional current, which runs the opposite way.
d_4C_1.plain: Electrons are like kids leaving a crowded room (anode) through a hallway (wire) to an empty room (cathode).

ox: Wrong. This describes a galvanic cell. Also, oxidation never occurs at the cathode.
Wrong. Positive E°cell and negative ΔG describe a spontaneous galvanic cell. Electrolytic cells are the opposite.
Wrong. Reduction occurs at the cathode in every cell. Only the sign of the electrode changes in an electrolytic cell, not its process.
Correct. An electrolytic cell uses an external power source to drive a nonspontaneous reaction (ΔG > 0, E°cell < 0). Reduction still occurs at the cathode.

p: An electrolytic cell uses outside electrical energy to force a reaction that would not happen on its own. Its ΔG is positive and its E°cell is negative.
Roles stay fixed: reduction at the cathode, oxidation at the anode. Only the signs flip: the cathode is negative and the anode is positive.

mem: Electrolytic: ΔG > 0, E°cell < 0, needs power source
Reduction at cathode, oxidation at anode always
Galvanic: cathode positive; electrolytic: cathode negative
d_4C_5.mn: An Ox and Red Cat: Anode = Oxidation, Reduction = Cathode.
d_4C_5.trap: Assuming electrode roles flip in electrolytic cells. Only the signs flip.
d_4C_5.plain: Pushing a bike uphill takes your effort. The hill is still a hill; you are just working against it.

ox: Wrong. A positive ΔG° goes with a NEGATIVE E°, and K above 1 needs a negative ΔG°. This option contradicts itself. The trap is flipping the sign in ΔG° = -nFE0.
Wrong. Negative ΔG° is right, but it means K is greater than 1, not less. The trap is forgetting that ln K has the same sign as E°.
Wrong. Positive ΔG° and K below 1 describe a nonspontaneous reaction, which needs a negative E°. The question says E° is positive.
Correct. Positive E° makes ΔG° = -nFE0 negative. Negative ΔG° = -RT ln K means ln K is positive, so K is greater than 1.

concept.t: Cell potential, free energy and K
p: E° is the standard cell potential, the voltage a cell makes under standard conditions. ΔG° is the standard free energy change. Negative ΔG° means the reaction is spontaneous (it runs on its own).
K is the equilibrium constant. If K is above 1, products are favored. The three are linked: ΔG° = -nFE0 = -RT ln K. A positive E° means negative ΔG° and K above 1.

mem: E° positive = ΔG° negative = K greater than 1 = spontaneous
E° negative = ΔG° positive = K less than 1 = nonspontaneous
ΔG° = -nFE0 = -RT ln K

fm.f: ΔG° = -n F E°, where n = moles of electrons transferred, F = Faraday constant, E° = standard cell potential, ΔG° = standard free energy change
fm.v: E° is positive; n and F are always positive
fm.why: It links voltage to free energy, so the sign of E° gives the sign of ΔG°.
fm.nc: Only the sign matters, so no arithmetic is needed.

d_4C_9.trap: Mixing up the signs. The minus sign in ΔG° = -nFE0 flips positive E° into negative ΔG°.
d_4C_9.plain: Think of a ball rolling downhill. Positive E° is a downhill slope, so the ball (the reaction) rolls toward products on its own.

ox: Correct. Charging uses an outside power source to force the nonspontaneous reverse reaction. That makes the cell electrolytic.
Wrong. A galvanic cell is spontaneous and cannot be recharged just by swapping electrodes. Charging needs an external power source.
Wrong. A concentration cell runs on a concentration difference. Charging a battery reverses its chemistry, not a gradient.
Wrong. A fuel cell is continually fed fresh reactants. It is not a battery being recharged.

p: A galvanic cell releases energy from a spontaneous reaction, like a battery discharging. An electrolytic cell uses outside energy to force a nonspontaneous reaction.
A rechargeable battery is galvanic when it discharges and electrolytic when it charges.

mem: Discharging = galvanic (spontaneous, ΔG < 0)
Charging = electrolytic (nonspontaneous, needs power source)
Cathode is still where reduction occurs in both
d_4C_11.trap: Thinking the cell stays galvanic while charging.
d_4C_11.plain: A ball rolling downhill makes energy by itself (discharge). Pushing it back uphill takes your effort (charging).

ox: Wrong. This reverses it. The 1.0 M half-cell is the cathode, where Cu²⁺ is reduced to lower its concentration.
Correct. The dilute 0.1 M side is the anode. Cu is oxidized there, adding Cu²⁺ to raise its concentration. Electrons flow from 0.1 M to 1.0 M.
Wrong. Standard E° is zero, but the cell potential also depends on Q through the Nernst equation. Different concentrations give a nonzero E.
Wrong. Electrons flow from anode to cathode, so this is backward.

p: A concentration cell has the same metal and ion on both sides but at different concentrations. The cell tries to even them out.
The dilute side gains ions (oxidation, anode). The concentrated side loses ions (reduction, cathode). Electrons go from anode to cathode.

mem: Dilute side = anode; concentrated side = cathode
E°cell = 0 but E is greater than 0 when concentrations differ
Cell runs until concentrations are equal
d_4C_12.trap: Seeing E° = 0 and concluding no current.
d_4C_12.plain: Two cups of juice, one strong and one weak. Nature moves flavor from strong to weak. Here, the weak cup gets more stuff added and the strong cup gets thinned out.

ox: Correct. With the object beyond 2f, the lens bends light to a real image between f and 2f on the far side. It is upside down (inverted) and smaller than the object.
Wrong. A virtual, upright, larger image is the magnifying-glass case, which needs the object inside f. The trap is mixing up the object zones.
Wrong. Real, inverted, larger happens when the object is between f and 2f. Students swap the two zones.
Wrong. No image forms (rays come out parallel) when the object sits exactly at f, not beyond 2f.

p: A converging lens bends light rays toward a point. f is the focal length, the distance where parallel rays meet. 2f is twice that distance. A real image is one that light actually reaches, so it can be shown on a screen.
Far objects (beyond 2f) make small, upside-down, real images. As the object moves closer, the image grows.

mem: Beyond 2f: real, inverted, smaller, image between f and 2f
At 2f: real, inverted, same size, image at 2f
Between f and 2f: real, inverted, larger
Inside f: virtual, upright, larger

tb.cap: Object position for a converging lens

q57.trap: Mixing up which zone gives a smaller image and which gives a larger one. Far object means small image.
q57.plain: Think of a camera photographing a faraway tree. The picture on the sensor is tiny and upside down.

ox: Correct. The moving ambulance squeezes the sound waves in front of it. Shorter wavelength means higher frequency, so you hear a higher pitch (Doppler effect).
Wrong. Lower pitch is heard when the source moves away. The trap is reversing the direction.
Wrong. Loudness (amplitude) may change, but the question asks about pitch, and pitch (frequency) does change. The option wrongly says it stays the same.
Wrong. The pitch is higher, but the reason is false. Sound speed is set by the medium (air), not by the moving source.

p: Frequency is how many waves reach your ear each second. Your brain hears frequency as pitch. When a source moves toward you, each new wave starts closer to you, so the waves bunch up.
Bunched waves have a shorter wavelength and a higher frequency. The wave speed stays the same because it depends only on the medium.

mem: Toward you: higher frequency, higher pitch
Away from you: lower frequency, lower pitch
Wave speed depends on the medium, not the source
q58.trap: Saying sound speeds up. The speed does not change; the wavelength shrinks.
q58.plain: Imagine a friend tossing balls to you while running toward you. The balls arrive more often than if he stood still.

ox: Correct. Photon energy is E = hf. Ultraviolet has the highest frequency of these choices, so it has the most energy.
Wrong. Red visible light has a lower frequency than UV, so less energy. Red is the lowest-energy visible color.
Wrong. Infrared sits below visible light in frequency, so its photons carry less energy.
Wrong. Microwaves have the lowest frequency here, so the least energy. The trap is picking the one that sounds most powerful, like microwave ovens.

p: Light comes in packets called photons. Each photon's energy equals Planck's constant (h) times its frequency (f). Higher frequency means more energy.
From low to high energy: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, γ.

mem: E = hf = hc/wavelength
High frequency means short wavelength and high energy
Order: radio, micro, IR, visible, UV, X-ray, γ

fm.f: E = hf, where E = photon energy, h = Planck's constant, f = frequency
fm.v: h is the same for all photons; UV has the largest f of the choices
fm.s: Largest f gives largest E, so UV
fm.why: Energy is directly proportional to frequency.
fm.nc: No numbers needed; just compare frequencies.

q59.mn: Roy G. Biv orders visible light: Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet. Red has the least energy and violet the most.
q59.trap: Confusing wavelength with energy. Longer wavelength means lower energy.
q59.plain: Think of shaking a rope. Faster shaking (higher frequency) puts more energy into each wiggle.

ox: Wrong. Decibels use a logarithm, so a 100-fold intensity change is not +100 dB. The trap is treating the scale as linear.
Correct. The change in level is 10 x log(100) = 10 × 2 = 20 dB.
Wrong. The log of 100 is 2, but you must multiply by 10. This answer forgets the factor of 10.
Wrong. Decibel changes add or subtract. They are not multiplied, since the scale is logarithmic.

p: The decibel (dB) scale measures sound level using a logarithm. A logarithm asks: 10 to what power gives this number? So log of 100 is 2.
Because of this, multiplying intensity by a factor adds a fixed number of dB. Each factor of 10 adds 10 dB.

mem: Factor of 10 in intensity = +10 dB
Factor of 100 = +20 dB; factor of 1000 = +30 dB
dB changes add; intensities multiply

fm.f: change in dB = 10 x log(I₂/I₁), where I₁ = starting intensity, I₂ = new intensity, log = power of 10
fm.why: Sound level is defined on a logarithmic scale.
fm.nc: Count the zeros in 100 (two), then multiply by 10.

q60.sc: Count the zeros in the intensity factor and multiply by 10 dB each.
q60.trap: Treating decibels as linear, or forgetting the 10 in front of the log.
q60.plain: Like a video game where each level needs 10 times more points. The level number goes up by 1 while the points jump 10-fold.

ox: Correct. A strong, sharp peak near 1710 cm⁻¹ is the signature of a C=O (carbonyl) stretch in a ketone, aldehyde, or similar group.
Wrong. An alcohol O-H gives a broad peak around 3200-3550 cm⁻¹, and the question says that peak is absent.
Wrong. A nitrile C triple bond N stretch appears near 2250 cm⁻¹, not 1710.
Wrong. An alkyne C-H gives a sharp peak near 3300 cm⁻¹, far from 1710. Students match any 'sharp' peak without checking the position.

p: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy shows which bonds are in a molecule. Each bond vibrates at a set wavenumber (cm⁻¹). A peak at that position tells you the bond is there.
The key peaks: C=O near 1700 (strong, sharp), O-H near 3300 (broad), C triple bond N near 2250.

mem: C=O: ~1700 cm⁻¹, strong and sharp
O-H alcohol: ~3300 cm⁻¹, broad; carboxylic acid O-H is even broader
C triple bond N: ~2250; C triple bond C: ~2100-2250
N-H: ~3300, sharper than O-H
q61.trap: Choosing by shape alone. Check both position and shape.
q61.plain: Each bond is like a guitar string with its own note. The spectrum shows which notes are playing.

ox: Wrong. Neutron-to-proton conversion is β decay and does not explain why a stable nucleus weighs less than its parts.
Wrong. Nucleons are conserved; none vanish.
Correct. When nucleons bind together, energy is released (the binding energy). By E = mc² this energy corresponds to lost mass, so the nucleus weighs less than the separate nucleons.
Wrong. Electron shielding is an atomic effect, not a nuclear one, and does not change nuclear mass.

p: The mass defect is the small difference between the mass of the separate protons and neutrons and the mass of the nucleus they form. The nucleus is lighter.

The missing mass was released as energy when the nucleus formed. E = mc² links the two, where c is the speed of light. That energy is the binding energy, which would be needed to pull the nucleus apart.

mem: Nucleus mass < sum of nucleon masses
Mass defect x c² = binding energy
Greater binding energy per nucleon means more stable
d_4E_9.trap: Thinking the missing mass means particles were destroyed.
d_4E_9.plain: Like a magnet set that gives off a click of energy when it snaps together. To break it apart, you must put that energy back.

ox: Correct. Level gaps shrink as n rises, so the 2-to-1 gap is bigger than the 3-to-2 gap. A bigger gap gives a photon with more energy and a shorter wavelength.
Wrong. Less energy would indeed pair with longer wavelength, but the 2-to-1 gap is the larger one.
Wrong. This pairs high energy with long wavelength, which cannot happen because E = hc/wavelength. Energy and wavelength move in opposite directions.
Wrong. Different transitions have different gaps and give photons of different energy. Assuming equal energy is the trap.

p: An electron in an atom sits in levels numbered n = 1, 2, 3 and so on. When it drops to a lower level, it releases a photon whose energy equals the gap between the levels.
The levels are close together at high n and far apart near n = 1. So jumps to or from n = 1 are the biggest.

mem: Photon energy = energy gap between levels
Gaps shrink as n increases
Bigger energy means shorter wavelength
d_4E_12.trap: Assuming every drop to a lower level releases the same energy.
d_4E_12.plain: Like stairs that get taller near the ground floor. Dropping the last step to the ground is the biggest drop.

ox: Correct. Ionization energy (energy to remove an electron) rises across a period. Neon, a noble gas with a full shell, holds its electrons most tightly of these choices.
Wrong. Sodium has one loosely held outer electron, so its ionization energy is very low.
Wrong. Magnesium is a metal, with a low ionization energy compared with the nonmetals.

Wrong. Fluorine is high, but neon sits one step further right in the same period with a filled shell and a higher value. The trap is confusing electronegativity (fluorine highest) with ionization energy.

p: First ionization energy is the energy needed to pull off the outermost electron from an atom. It is high when the electron is held tightly.
