Across a period (left to right) the nucleus gains protons, so the pull grows. Up a group, atoms are smaller, so it also grows. Helium and neon are the top.

mem: Ionization energy increases left to right and bottom to top
Noble gases are highest in their period
Metals lose electrons easily
d_4E_14.trap: Picking fluorine because it has the highest electronegativity. Noble gases are excluded from electronegativity but top ionization energy.
d_4E_14.plain: Like pulling a toy from a child's hand. A child gripping it tightly (neon) is hardest to beat.

ox: Wrong. Neon has a full shell, so it does not want another electron. Its electron affinity is near zero or unfavorable.
Wrong. Sodium gains an electron only weakly. It prefers to lose one.
Wrong. Magnesium has a filled 3s subshell, so adding an electron is near zero or unfavorable.

Correct. Chlorine is one electron short of a full octet and strongly attracts one. Its electron affinity is the most exothermic of these (and even more than fluorine, whose tiny size causes crowding).

p: Electron affinity is the energy change when an atom gains an electron. If energy is released (exothermic), the atom likes the extra electron.
Halogens are one electron from a full outer shell, so they have the strongest affinities. Noble gases and filled subshells do not want another electron.

mem: Halogens have the most exothermic electron affinity
Chlorine slightly beats fluorine
Noble gases and Group 2 are near zero
d_4E_16.trap: Assuming fluorine must be highest in everything. Its small size makes electron crowding.
d_4E_16.plain: Like a puzzle missing one piece. The piece snaps in happily. A finished puzzle (neon) has no space.

ox: Correct. Hund's rule says electrons fill separate orbitals of equal energy first, all with the same (parallel) spin. Nitrogen's three 2p electrons sit in three different p orbitals, spins parallel.
Wrong. Pairing two electrons in one p orbital while another stays empty breaks Hund's rule. The trap is pairing too early.
Wrong. Separate orbitals is right, but spins should be parallel. Antiparallel spins lose the stability Hund's rule gives.
Wrong. Three electrons cannot be fully paired in two orbitals; one would be unpaired. Pairs need two electrons each.

p: The three 2p orbitals have the same energy. Hund's rule says electrons spread out one per orbital, all spinning the same way, before any pair up.
This lowers repulsion between electrons. Nitrogen therefore has three unpaired electrons, making it paramagnetic.

mem: Fill degenerate orbitals singly first, parallel spins
Pair up only after every orbital has one electron
Unpaired electrons mean paramagnetic
d_4E_20.trap: Pairing electrons before every orbital in the subshell has one.
d_4E_20.plain: Like kids on a bus choosing seats. Each takes an empty row first before anyone sits beside another.

ox: Wrong. pH 1 would be 0.1 M HCl. Check the exponent.
Correct. HCl is a strong acid, so it fully dissociates and [H⁺] = 0.01 = 10⁻² M, giving pH = 2.
Wrong. 12 is the pOH for this solution (14 − 2), not the pH.
Wrong. 0.01 is the concentration, not the pH. pH is the negative log of it.

p: pH = -log[H⁺], where [H⁺] is the hydrogen ion concentration in moles per liter. A strong acid breaks apart completely in water.
So [H⁺] equals the acid concentration. 0.01 M HCl gives [H⁺] = 10⁻², and pH = 2.

mem: Strong acids: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₄.
pH + pOH = 14.
Each 10x change in [H⁺] changes pH by 1.

fm.why: A strong acid fully dissociates, so [H⁺] equals its concentration.
fm.nc: Write the concentration as a power of 10; the pH is the exponent without the minus sign.

q67.trap: Confusing pH with pOH, or with the concentration value itself.
q67.plain: pH just counts the zeros in the decimal. 0.01 has the 1 in the second place, so pH is 2.

ox: Wrong. This is the pH when the base to acid ratio is 1:10 (more acid than base).
Correct. Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKₐ + log(10) = pKₐ + 1.
Wrong. pH equals pKₐ only when [A-] = [HA], a ratio of 1.
Wrong. The relationship is logarithmic, so a ratio of 10 adds 1, not 10.

p: A buffer has a weak acid (HA) and its conjugate base (A-). The equation links pH to the ratio of the two.
When base is 10 times acid, log(10) = 1, so pH is one unit above pKₐ. pKₐ is the pH where acid and base are equal.

mem: pH = pKₐ + log([A-]/[HA]).
Ratio 1 gives pH = pKₐ; ratio 10 gives pKₐ + 1; ratio 0.1 gives pKₐ - 1.
More base than acid means pH above pKₐ.

fm.f: pH = pKₐ + log([A-]/[HA]), where pKₐ = -log of the acid dissociation constant, [A-] = base concentration, [HA] = acid concentration
fm.why: This is the buffer equation, and the question gives the ratio.
fm.nc: log(10) = 1, so no calculator is needed.

q68.sc: Ratio 10x means plus 1; 100x means plus 2; 1/10 means minus 1.
q68.trap: Reversing the ratio (acid over base) or treating the log as linear.
q68.plain: A seesaw balanced at pKₐ tilts one notch for each factor of 10 you pile on the base side.

ox: Wrong. Glucose does not dissociate, so i = 1 and the effect is proportional to 0.1.
Wrong. NaCl gives 2 particles (Na⁺ and Cl⁻), so i = 2 and the effect is proportional to 0.2.
Correct. CaCl₂ gives 3 particles (Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻), so i = 3 and the effect is proportional to 0.3, the largest.
Wrong. MgSO₄ gives 2 particles, so 2 × 0.05 = 0.1, which is smaller than 0.3.

p: Dissolved particles lower a solvent's freezing point. This is a colligative property, meaning it depends on the number of particles, not their identity.
Compare i x molality, where i is the number of particles one formula unit makes. The largest product gives the lowest freezing point.

mem: Colligative: depends on particle count.
Typical i: glucose 1, NaCl 2, CaCl₂ 3.
Higher i x m means lower freezing point.

fm.f: dTf = i x Kf x m, where dTf = freezing point drop, i = particles per formula unit, Kf = solvent constant, m = molality (mol/kg)
fm.v: Compare i x m: glucose 1 × 0.1, NaCl 2 × 0.1, CaCl₂ 3 × 0.1, MgSO₄ 2 × 0.05
fm.why: Kf is the same for water, so only i x m differs.
fm.nc: Multiply small numbers by hand; Kf cancels in the comparison.

q69.sc: Just compare i x m; skip Kf.
q69.trap: Forgetting to multiply by i, or choosing the highest molality.
q69.plain: The more people crowd onto a dance floor, the harder it is for water molecules to line up and freeze.

ox: Correct. NaCl adds Cl⁻, which AgCl also makes when it dissolves. By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts toward solid AgCl, so less AgCl dissolves.
Wrong. This treats the added salt as helping dissolve things. A shared (common) ion does the opposite and suppresses dissolving.
Wrong. It is true that Kₛₚ stays constant, which is the trap. But Kₛₚ = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] stays fixed while [Cl⁻] rises, so [Ag⁺] must fall, and solubility changes.
Wrong. Kₛₚ is an equilibrium constant that changes only with temperature, not with added ions.

p: Solubility is how much solid dissolves. AgCl dissolves a tiny bit: AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻. The Kₛₚ is the product [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] at equilibrium (brackets mean concentration).
If you add a salt with one of the same ions (Cl⁻ from NaCl), the product is pushed too high. The system fixes this by making more solid AgCl, so less dissolves.

mem: Adding a common ion lowers solubility.
Kₛₚ changes only with temperature.
Kₛₚ = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] for AgCl.
q70.sc: See a shared ion added? Pick 'solubility decreases'.
q70.trap: Confusing solubility with Kₛₚ. Kₛₚ stays constant; solubility shifts.
q70.plain: A bus has a fixed number of seats. If lots of people are already standing in the aisle (extra Cl⁻), fewer new people can get on.

ox: Correct. At equivalence all the weak acid has become its conjugate base (A⁻). A⁻ takes H⁺ from water, making OH⁻, so the pH is above 7.
Wrong. pH 7 at equivalence is only for a strong acid with a strong base, where neither product reacts with water.
Wrong. Below 7 happens when a weak base is titrated with a strong acid, because the conjugate acid is left over.
Wrong. pH = pKₐ is at the half-equivalence point, where half the acid has been converted. Equivalence is later.

p: The equivalence point is when moles of base added equal the moles of acid you started with. For a weak acid HA, all of it is turned into A⁻, its conjugate base (the particle left after losing H⁺).
A⁻ is a weak base. It grabs H⁺ from water, leaving extra OH⁻. More OH⁻ means the pH is above 7.

mem: Weak acid + strong base: equivalence pH > 7.
Weak base + strong acid: equivalence pH < 7.
Strong + strong: pH = 7.
Half-equivalence: pH = pKₐ.
q71.trap: Assuming equivalence always means pH 7. Look at what is left: the conjugate of the weak partner decides.
q71.plain: After the fight is over, the winner (the stronger side) still leaves a little mess. Here the leftover is a mild base.

ox: Wrong. Two mistakes. Dispersion is placed first, but for comparable small molecules it is the weakest. Hydrogen bonds are also placed above ion-dipole, but a full charge pulling on a polar molecule is stronger. (Ion-dipole above dipole-dipole is actually right.)
Wrong. Dipole-dipole is weaker than ion-dipole and hydrogen bonds, and hydrogen bonds are not the weakest. This order is scrambled.
Correct. Full charges give the strongest pull (ion-dipole), then hydrogen bonds, then permanent dipoles (dipole-dipole), then London dispersion, which comes from short-lived induced dipoles.
Wrong. It puts hydrogen bonds above ion-dipole and dispersion above dipole-dipole. Both pairs are in the wrong order.

p: Intermolecular forces are attractions between separate molecules. The more charge involved, the stronger the pull. An ion has a full charge, so ion-dipole (an ion near a polar molecule) is strongest.

A hydrogen bond is a special strong dipole-dipole between H on N, O or F and a lone pair. Ordinary dipole-dipole is next. London dispersion (temporary dipoles in any molecule) is weakest for small molecules.

mem: Order: ion-dipole > H-bond > dipole-dipole > London.
H-bond needs H on N, O or F.
London grows with molecule size and electron count.
d_5B_14.trap: Students forget that ion-dipole outranks hydrogen bonds, because full charges pull harder than partial charges.
d_5B_14.plain: Think of magnets. A big fridge magnet is an ion pulling on a polar molecule. A medium magnet is a hydrogen bond. A small craft magnet is a regular dipole-dipole pull. A weak sticker is London dispersion.

ox: Wrong. Base pairs are held by hydrogen bonds, which are non-covalent. Covalent bonds hold the backbone together.
Correct. G-C has three hydrogen bonds and A-T has two, and G-C stacks more strongly. More energy (higher temperature) is needed to pull the strands apart.
Wrong. Phosphates are in the sugar-phosphate backbone, not in the pairing. Each nucleotide has one, so the count does not differ by base.
Wrong. Both G and A are purines (two rings). The pyrimidines are C, T and U. This also would not explain melting.

p: Melting temperature (Tm) is the temperature at which half of the double-stranded DNA has separated into single strands. Strands come apart when hydrogen bonds between bases break.
Guanine pairs with cytosine using three hydrogen bonds. Adenine pairs with thymine using two. More hydrogen bonds means more heat needed, so more G-C means a higher Tm.

mem: G-C: 3 H-bonds. A-T: 2 H-bonds.
More G-C content means higher Tm.
Purines: A, G. Pyrimidines: C, T, U.
d_5B_17.mn: Pure As Gold: Purines are Adenine and Guanine. CUT the Pie: Cytosine, Uracil, Thymine are pyrimidines.
d_5B_17.trap: Mixing up the hydrogen bond counts, or saying the bases are joined covalently.
d_5B_17.plain: Two sheets held together by three pieces of tape are harder to pull apart than two held by two pieces.

ox: Correct. For water, the solid-liquid line slopes backward (negative slope). Raising pressure at a temperature just below 0 C moves you across the line into the liquid region, so ice melts.
Wrong. Where the triple point sits does not explain pressure melting. The slope of the solid-liquid line does.
Wrong. The critical point is about liquid and gas becoming one fluid. It has nothing to do with ice melting.
Wrong. Sublimation (solid to gas) curves slope upward, and this question is about solid to liquid.

p: A phase diagram plots pressure (up) against temperature (across) and shows which phase (solid, liquid, gas) is stable. The lines are where two phases coexist.

For most substances the solid-liquid line leans right. For water it leans left, because ice is less dense than liquid water. Pressure favors the denser phase, which is liquid, so squeezing ice makes it melt.

mem: Water's solid-liquid line has a negative slope.
Ice is less dense than liquid water.
Pressure favors the denser phase.
d_5B_20.trap: Assuming the solid-liquid line always slopes forward as in most substances like CO₂.
d_5B_20.plain: Ice takes up more room than water. Squeeze it and it prefers to turn into water, which is more compact.

ox: Wrong. Complete transfer describes an ionic bond. In a coordinate bond the pair is still shared between N and B.
Correct. In H₃N-BF₃ the nitrogen lone pair supplies both electrons to boron, which has an empty p orbital. N is the Lewis base (electron donor) and B is the Lewis acid (electron acceptor).
Wrong. One electron from each atom is the ordinary covalent bond. In a coordinate bond both electrons come from one atom.
Wrong. The shared pair sits between N and B. The fluorines are on boron and do not donate it.

p: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons. Usually each atom gives one electron. In a coordinate (dative) bond, one atom gives both electrons.
A Lewis base has a lone pair to give. A Lewis acid has an empty orbital to accept it. Boron in BF₃ has only 6 electrons, so it accepts the lone pair from NH₃.

mem: Coordinate bond: both electrons from one atom.
Lewis base donates a pair, Lewis acid accepts.
Once formed, it acts like any covalent bond.
x5B_004.trap: Thinking the bond is different in kind after forming. It is only different in where the electrons came from.
x5B_004.plain: Two friends share a sandwich. Usually each brings half. In a coordinate bond, one friend brought the whole sandwich and the other brought the empty plate.

ox: Wrong. Forming a bond releases energy, so potential energy falls. It does not rise to the bond and stay flat.
Wrong. Even without gaining or losing electrons, attraction of each electron to both nuclei lowers the energy as the atoms approach.
Wrong. Energy does not keep falling. At very short distances, the two positive nuclei repel strongly and energy shoots up.

Correct. Energy drops as the atoms approach and reaches a minimum at the bond length (the stable distance). Closer than that, nuclear repulsion makes it rise sharply. The depth of the well is the bond energy.

p: Potential energy is stored energy from position. Far apart, two H atoms do not interact, so energy is about zero. As they approach, electrons are attracted to both nuclei and energy goes down.
At the bond length the pull and push balance, giving the lowest energy. Closer than that, the positive nuclei repel each other and energy rises steeply.

mem: Bond length = minimum of the energy curve.
Depth of the well = bond energy.
Too close: nuclear repulsion dominates.
x5B_005.trap: Picking 'continuously decreases'. Repulsion at short range makes the curve turn back up.
x5B_005.plain: Two magnets pulled together settle in a sweet spot. Push them any closer and something shoves back.

ox: Wrong. DNA does not go to the cathode, and larger fragments move slower, so both parts are wrong.
Wrong. The direction (anode) is right, but larger fragments move slower, not faster. Big pieces get stuck in the gel pores.
Correct. DNA's phosphate backbone is negative, so it moves toward the positive anode. Smaller fragments wiggle through the gel pores faster, so they travel farther.
Wrong. Negative DNA is repelled by the negative cathode, so the direction is wrong. The size part is right.

p: Electrophoresis uses an electric field to move charged molecules through a gel. DNA has a negative charge from its phosphate backbone, so it runs toward the positive electrode (anode).
The gel is a mesh of tiny pores. Small fragments slip through quickly, large ones get slowed down. After a run, small pieces sit near the far end.

mem: DNA is negative, so it moves to the anode (+).
Smaller fragments travel farther.
Charge-to-mass is the same for all DNA, so size decides speed.
d_5C_21.mn: Opposites attract: negative DNA runs to the positive pole.
d_5C_21.trap: Forgetting DNA is negative, or reversing which size moves faster.
d_5C_21.plain: Like running through a thick forest. A small kid darts between trees fast, but a kid carrying a big sheet gets stuck.

ox: Wrong. Two liquids with close boiling points need fractional distillation, not sublimation.
Correct. A solid with significant vapor pressure below its melting point turns straight to gas, then re-deposits on a cold surface as pure crystals. Nonvolatile impurities stay behind.
Wrong. A dissolved salt is recovered by evaporating the water or by crystallization. Salt does not sublime.
Wrong. Proteins differing in mass are separated by chromatography or electrophoresis. Proteins do not vaporize.

p: Sublimation is a solid turning directly into a gas without becoming liquid. Some solids, like iodine, caffeine or naphthalene, have enough vapor pressure to do this when heated gently.
Collect the gas on a cold surface and it becomes solid again, pure. Impurities that cannot vaporize stay behind.

mem: Sublimation: solid to gas directly.
Deposition: gas to solid directly.
Works if the solid is volatile and impurities are not.
d_5C_28.trap: Thinking sublimation applies only to dry ice. Many other solids can be purified this way.
d_5C_28.plain: Like frost on a cold window. Water vapor in the air skips being liquid and sticks as ice, leaving dust behind.

ox: Correct. Two liquids that do not mix stack by density. Ether is 0.71 g/mL and water is 1.00 g/mL, so the lighter ether floats on top.
Wrong. The idea that organic layers always sink is false. They sink only if denser than water, like dichloromethane. Ether is lighter.
Wrong. Polarity decides whether liquids mix, not which one is on top. Also, ether is less polar than water, so the reasoning is backward.
Wrong. Ether and water are largely immiscible, so they form two layers. They do not make one mixed phase.

p: A separatory funnel holds two liquids that do not mix (immiscible). They form two layers. The denser liquid (more mass per mL) goes to the bottom.
Density is the only thing that decides which layer is on top. Water is 1.00 g/mL. Any liquid below 1.00 floats on water. Any liquid above 1.00 sinks.

mem: Top layer = lower density
Water is 1.00 g/mL
Ether, hexane, ethyl acetate float on water
Dichloromethane and chloroform sink below water
x5C_002.trap: Assuming organic means top. Always compare the density number to 1.00.
x5C_002.plain: Oil floats on water in a salad dressing bottle. The lighter liquid always rides on top.

ox: Wrong. This assumes organic solvents always float. Dichloromethane is 1.33 g/mL, denser than water, so the organic layer is on the bottom.
Wrong. Water (1.00 g/mL) is the top layer here, and it is the aqueous phase. Keeping it would throw away the product, which moved into the organic layer.
Wrong. The product does not split evenly. A neutral organic compound strongly prefers the organic solvent, so it is mostly in one layer.
Correct. Dichloromethane (1.33) is denser than water (1.00), so the organic layer sits at the bottom. The product moved there, so drain the bottom layer through the stopcock and keep it.

p: In an extraction, the product moves into the solvent it likes best. A neutral organic product moves into the organic solvent.
Then you must find which layer that is. Compare density to water (1.00 g/mL). Denser solvents like dichloromethane sit on the bottom and are drained out first.

mem: Bottom layer = denser liquid
Dichloromethane is denser than water, so it is the bottom layer
Neutral organic products go into the organic layer
Never throw away a layer until you have found your product
x5C_003.trap: Assuming the organic layer is always on top. Check density first.
x5C_003.plain: It is like knowing which shelf holds your toy. First find which liquid is heavier, then you know which layer is at the bottom.

ox: Wrong. Bicarbonate is a weak base (its conjugate acid has pKₐ about 6.4). It cannot pull the proton off a phenol (pKₐ about 10). It removes only stronger acids like carboxylic acids.
Correct. Hydroxide is a strong base (conjugate acid water, pKₐ about 15.7). It removes the phenol's proton, making charged phenoxide, which dissolves in water. Naphthalene stays in the ether.
Wrong. Acid keeps the phenol protonated and neutral, so it stays in the ether. HCl would remove bases such as amines instead.
Wrong. Brine (salt water) just helps dry the organic layer. It does not react with the phenol.

p: A neutral molecule dissolves in organic solvent. A charged molecule (an ion) dissolves in water. To move an acid into water, add a base strong enough to remove its proton and make it an ion.
The base works only if its conjugate acid has a higher pKₐ than the acid you are removing. Phenol pKₐ is about 10, so you need hydroxide.

mem: Carboxylic acid pKₐ about 4-5: NaHCO₃ works
Phenol pKₐ about 10: needs NaOH
Base converts an acid to a water-soluble salt
HCl pulls amines into water
x5C_004.trap: Using bicarbonate for a phenol. It is too weak. Compare the pKₐ values.
x5C_004.plain: It is like putting a floaty vest on someone so they leave the oil pool and move into the water pool. Only a strong enough push (base) does it.

ox: Correct. Each carbon has H, Br, CH₃ and the other CHBr group. An internal mirror plane makes the molecule meso. Because the ends are identical, (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) are the same molecule numbered from opposite ends.
Wrong. Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images. A meso compound is superimposable on its own mirror image, so the inversion gives the same molecule.
Wrong. A racemic mixture is a 50:50 mix of two chiral enantiomers. This compound is achiral, so no such pair exists.
Wrong. Diastereomers are different compounds. Changing both centers of a meso compound gives the same compound, not a different one.

p: A stereocenter is a carbon with four different groups. A meso compound has stereocenters but is not chiral, because it has an internal mirror plane. Its mirror image is itself.
In 2,3-dibromobutane, both stereocenters hold the same set of groups. So the R,S form is the same as S,R. The R,R and S,S forms are the real enantiomer pair.

mem: Meso: stereocenters plus an internal mirror plane, so achiral
In a meso compound with two centers, the labels are opposite (R,S)
2,3-dibromobutane has 3 stereoisomers: R,R / S,S enantiomers and one meso
x5D_014.trap: Assuming opposite labels always mean enantiomers. If the molecule is symmetric, they are identical.
x5D_014.plain: Your two hands are mirror images but different. A symmetric mug is its own mirror image. A meso compound is like the mug.

ox: Correct. In trans-1,2, one methyl points up and the other down on adjacent carbons. A chair can put both in equatorial positions, which is the roomy position.
Wrong. For cis-1,2 both groups point the same way, so on adjacent carbons one is axial and one is equatorial in either chair.
Wrong. For 1,3, the cis isomer is the diequatorial one. The trans isomer always has one axial group.
Wrong. For 1,4, the trans isomer is diequatorial. The cis isomer always has one axial group.

p: In a chair, each carbon has an axial position (straight up or down) and an equatorial position (out to the side). Equatorial is roomier, so large groups prefer it.
Rule of thumb: 1,2 and 1,4 substitution: trans can be diequatorial. 1,3 substitution: cis can be diequatorial.

mem: 1,2: trans = diequatorial
1,3: cis = diequatorial
1,4: trans = diequatorial
Cis on 1,2 / 1,4 or trans on 1,3 always leaves one group axial
x5D_023.sc: Look at the second number. Even (2 or 4): trans is diequatorial. Odd (3): cis is diequatorial. So 1,2 and 1,4 trans; 1,3 cis.
x5D_023.trap: Applying one rule to all positions. The 1,3 pattern is reversed from 1,2 and 1,4.
x5D_023.plain: Like sitting at a crowded table, the groups want the open outside seats (equatorial) rather than the cramped seats pointing up or down (axial).

ox: Wrong. The two salts are not mirror images, so they are not enantiomers. Enantiomers would have identical solubilities and could not be separated.
Wrong. The amine does not change the acid's configuration. Racemization would not help separation anyway.
Correct. The (R)-amine pairs with R-acid to give (R,R) and with S-acid to give (S,R). These are not mirror images, so they are diastereomers with different solubilities. One crystallizes first.
Wrong. Both enantiomers of the acid react with the amine, forming two different salts. It is the salts that differ.

p: Enantiomers have identical physical properties, so you cannot separate them by crystallization. Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images, and they do differ in solubility and melting point.
Reacting a racemic acid with a pure chiral amine gives two diastereomeric salts. Crystallize one out, then add strong acid to free the pure acid.

mem: Racemic acid + pure chiral amine gives diastereomeric salts
Diastereomers: different solubility, so crystallize
Recover the acid by adding strong acid
x5D_025.trap: Calling the salts enantiomers. The amine's fixed handedness makes them diastereomers.
x5D_025.plain: Two left shoes look alike to a table. Match each with a right shoe of a different size and the pairs now look different, so they can be sorted.

ox: Wrong. Meso compounds need two or more stereocenters with symmetry. This product has only one stereocenter, so it is chiral.

Correct. A tertiary halide in water reacts by SN1. The leaving group leaves first and gives a flat carbocation. Water can attack from either face, so both R and S alcohols form and the mixture is nearly racemic.
Wrong. Pure inversion is the SN2 outcome. A crowded tertiary carbon cannot be attacked from the back.
Wrong. Pure retention would need the carbocation to remember its shape. A flat cation does not, so both faces are open.

p: In SN1, the leaving group leaves first, making a carbocation. A carbocation carbon is sp2 and flat. The nucleophile (here water) can attack from either face.
Attack from both faces gives both enantiomers, so a chiral starting material gives a racemic or nearly racemic product. Tertiary carbons and polar protic solvents favor SN1.

mem: Tertiary + polar protic solvent + weak nucleophile: SN1
Planar carbocation gives racemization
SN2 gives inversion; SN1 gives racemization
x5D_027.trap: Choosing inversion because it is the best-known substitution outcome. Inversion belongs to SN2.
x5D_027.plain: Picture a flat pancake you can flip from either side. After the flip you cannot tell which side was originally up.

ox: Wrong. I- is the best nucleophile in protic solvents, where small anions are caged by hydrogen bonds. In DMSO there is no such caging, so that order flips. This is the classic trap.
Correct. DMSO has no O-H or N-H to hydrogen bond to anions, so the anions are bare. Then nucleophilicity follows basicity, and F- is the strongest base of the halides.
Wrong. Cl⁻ is a weaker base than F-, so in a non-hydrogen-bonding solvent it is less nucleophilic.
Wrong. Br⁻ is a weaker base than F- and Cl⁻, so it ranks below them in aprotic solvents.

p: A polar protic solvent has O-H or N-H bonds (water, alcohols). It surrounds anions with hydrogen bonds, which hides small anions like F-. A polar aprotic solvent (DMSO, acetone) has no such bonds, so anions are free.
With free anions, a stronger base is a stronger nucleophile. So in aprotic solvents: F- > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I-. In protic solvents the order reverses.

mem: Protic solvent: I- > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F-
Aprotic solvent: F- > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I-
Aprotic: nucleophilicity tracks basicity
x5D_029.trap: Using the protic-solvent order. Read the solvent first.
x5D_029.plain: In water, F- is wrapped in a heavy blanket of water molecules and cannot move well. In DMSO it has no blanket, so it runs freely.

ox: Wrong. This describes the difference threshold (just noticeable difference), which compares two stimuli. Absolute threshold involves one stimulus.
Wrong. Because of neural noise, no intensity is detected every single time. Detection is probabilistic.
Correct. The absolute threshold is the minimum intensity of a stimulus detected 50% of the time.
Wrong. That is a pain threshold. Absolute threshold is about first being able to detect something, not about pain.

p: The absolute threshold is the weakest stimulus a person can notice. A very faint stimulus is noticed on some tries and missed on others, because the nervous system is noisy.
So scientists define it as the intensity detected half the time (50%).

mem: Absolute threshold: minimum intensity detected 50% of the time
Difference threshold (JND): smallest detectable change between two stimuli
Detection is probabilistic, never a sharp cutoff
d_6A_3.trap: Mixing up absolute threshold (one stimulus) with the difference threshold (change between two).
d_6A_3.plain: Whispering from far away: your friend hears you about half the time. That distance is the threshold.

ox: Wrong. Habituation is a central (brain) decrease in response to a repeated stimulus. Nothing here involves an expectation, and the best match is receptor-level fading.
Correct. Sensory adaptation is when receptors respond less to a constant, unchanging stimulus, such as a steady odor.
Wrong. Nothing is damaged. A threshold rise from damage would not fade with time in a room and would not return when the odor changes.
Wrong. Selective attention is choosing what to focus on. The odor fades because receptors tire, not because focus moved.

p: Sensory adaptation means receptors fire less when a stimulus stays the same. This lets you notice changes instead of constant background.
Habituation is different. It happens in the brain: you learn to ignore a repeated harmless stimulus.

mem: Sensory adaptation: receptors respond less to constant stimulus
Habituation: brain-level decline from repetition
Selective attention: choosing what to focus on
d_6A_6.trap: Choosing habituation. On the MCAT, fading of a constant stimulus at the receptor is adaptation.
d_6A_6.plain: Walking into a bakery you smell bread. After a few minutes your nose stops reporting it, like a friend who gets bored of the same news.

ox: Correct. Hair cells of the organ of Corti bend against the tectorial membrane. This opens ion channels and makes the cell depolarize, turning movement into a neural signal (transduction).
Wrong. The ossicles (three tiny ear bones) amplify vibration and push on the oval window, not the round window. They do not make neural signals.
Wrong. Photoreceptors are in the retina and detect light. The cochlea has hair cells.
Wrong. The tympanic membrane (eardrum) only vibrates. It does not fire action potentials.

p: Transduction means turning one type of energy into nerve signals. Sound is a mechanical vibration. The eardrum and ossicles pass it along as mechanical movement only.
In the cochlea, fluid waves move the basilar membrane. Hair cells on it bend against the tectorial membrane, and that bending creates the neural signal.

mem: Transduction occurs in hair cells of the organ of Corti
Ossicles: malleus, incus, stapes, mechanical amplification
Stapes pushes on the oval window
d_6A_9.trap: Thinking the eardrum or ossicles do the conversion. They only move mechanically.
d_6A_9.plain: The eardrum and bones are like a drum and sticks passing a beat. The hair cells are the microphone that turns it into an electric signal.

ox: Wrong. This is the difference threshold (JND), the smallest noticeable change between two stimuli.
Wrong. That is the pain threshold, a separate idea.
Correct. Absolute threshold is the minimum intensity detected on 50% of trials.
Wrong. Detection varies trial to trial because of neural noise, so 100% is not used. The 50% mark is the standard.

p: Near the weakest level you can sense, the same faint stimulus is noticed sometimes and missed other times. Random noise in the nervous system causes this.
So the absolute threshold is set at the intensity noticed on half (50%) of trials.

mem: Absolute threshold = minimum stimulus detected 50% of trials
JND = smallest change detected between two stimuli
Pain threshold is a different concept
x6A_001.trap: Choosing 100%. No intensity near threshold is detected every time.
x6A_001.plain: Like hearing a far-off whisper: some tries you catch it, some you do not. The distance where you catch it half the time is the threshold.

ox: Wrong. A larger Weber fraction (0.08) means a bigger relative change is needed, so brightness is discriminated less precisely. Trap: reading a bigger number as better.
Correct. Weight needs only a 2% change to be noticed, brightness needs 8%. A smaller fraction means finer relative discrimination.
Wrong. Weber fractions describe difference thresholds (changes between stimuli), not absolute thresholds.
Wrong. Weber fractions say nothing about how fast sensory adaptation occurs.

p: The Weber fraction is the proportion of change needed to notice a difference: JND divided by the starting intensity.
A small fraction means you notice tiny relative changes, so you are more sensitive. A large fraction means you need big changes.

fm.f: Weber fraction = JND / I, where JND = smallest noticeable change, I = starting intensity
fm.nc: Turn decimals into percents: 0.02 is 2%, 0.08 is 8%.

mem: Smaller Weber fraction means better discrimination
Weber fraction relates to difference thresholds only
x6A_004.trap: Thinking a larger number means more sensitive. It is the reverse.
x6A_004.plain: If you can spot a 2-cent change on a 100-cent snack, you are sharper than someone who needs an 8-cent change.

ox: Correct. Top-down processing uses context, memory, and expectation to interpret input. The sentence helps you read the misspelled word.
Wrong. Bottom-up starts with raw features such as lines and edges and builds up. Trap: the misspelling alone would make bottom-up reading hard.
Wrong. Parallel processing means handling many features at the same time. It does not describe using context. Trap: confusing a mechanism with a direction.
Wrong. Feature detection is the bottom-up step of picking out lines and edges. Trap: mixing this with expectation-driven reading.

p: Bottom-up processing starts with the raw sensory data and builds toward a perception. Top-down processing starts with knowledge and expectations that shape how data are read.
When context helps you read a misspelled word, your brain is filling in the answer from what it already knows. That is top-down.

mem: Top-down = expectations, context, memory
Bottom-up = raw features to perception
Parallel processing = many features at once
q93.trap: If context or experience guides perception, choose top-down.
q93.plain: Guessing a word in a story from the sentence around it, rather than sounding out every letter.

ox: Correct. The law of proximity says items that are close together are seen as a group.
Wrong. Similarity groups items that look alike, such as same color or shape. Here the cue is closeness. Trap: mixing up the two grouping cues.
Wrong. Closure fills in gaps so you see a complete shape. Trap: the 'gaps' idea can sound like distance.
Wrong. Continuity prefers smooth, continuous lines or paths. Trap: dots in a row can suggest a line, but here grouping is by closeness.

p: Gestalt psychology says the brain organizes parts into whole patterns. Several rules explain how we group things.
Proximity groups near items. Similarity groups alike items. Closure fills gaps. Continuity follows smooth lines.

mem: Proximity = near together
Similarity = look alike
Closure = fill in gaps
Continuity = smooth lines
q94.trap: Find the cue in the stem. 'Close together' always means proximity.
q94.plain: Kids standing close together at recess look like one team, even if they wear different shirts.

ox: Correct. Even though you were not attending to that conversation, your brain still processed it enough to catch your name. This is the cocktail party effect and shows unattended input gets some processing.
Wrong. You were not following that conversation, so this is not divided attention. Trap: being able to hear something does not mean you were attending to it.
Wrong. Inattentional blindness is failing to notice something visible because attention is elsewhere. Here you did notice. Trap: confusing failure to notice with noticing.
Wrong. Change blindness is missing a change in a scene. Nothing changed here. Trap: confusing attention-related terms.

concept.t: Selective attention and the cocktail party effect
p: Selective attention means focusing on one input and filtering out others. The cocktail party effect is hearing your own name or something important in a conversation you were ignoring.
This suggests unattended input is not fully blocked. It is partly analyzed for meaning, which fits attenuation models of attention.

mem: Cocktail party effect = hearing your name in an ignored conversation
Unattended info gets partial processing
Inattentional blindness = missing visible things when attention is elsewhere
q95.trap: Do not confuse noticing an ignored stimulus with the failures of attention such as inattentional or change blindness.
q95.plain: Chatting with a friend in a crowd, then turning your head when someone across the room says your name.

ox: Correct. REM sleep has vivid dreams, muscle atonia (temporary loss of muscle tone), and fast, wake-like EEG waves. It is also called paradoxical sleep.
Wrong. NREM stage 3 is slow-wave sleep with delta waves, the deepest NREM stage. Trap: deep sleep is not dreaming sleep.
Wrong. Stage 1 is light sleep with θ waves, as you drift off. Trap: the EEG slows here, not wake-like.
Wrong. Stage 2 has sleep spindles and K-complexes. Trap: it is the longest stage, but not the dreaming one.

p: Sleep alternates between NREM stages 1 to 3 and REM. EEG is a recording of brain waves.
REM is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs. Muscles are paralyzed so you do not act out dreams, and the brain waves look like those of wakefulness.

mem: REM: dreams, atonia, wake-like β/low-voltage EEG
Stage 1: θ; Stage 2: spindles and K-complexes
Stage 3: delta waves, slow-wave sleep
q96.mn: REM = Rapid Eye Movement. Also remember 'paradoxical sleep': the brain looks awake, but the body is paralyzed.
q96.trap: Wake-like EEG plus paralysis points to REM, not any NREM stage.
q96.plain: In REM the brain is busy like it is awake, but the body is switched off, like a movie playing on a remote-controlled TV.

ox: Correct. The NEW phone number (learned later) blocks recall of the OLD one. New learning reaching backward to disrupt old memory is retroactive interference.
Proactive interference is the reverse: an OLD memory blocks learning or recall of NEW information. Here the new number is blocking the old one, so direction is the trap.
Decay says memories fade just from time and disuse. The question gives a specific cause (learning a new number), which points to interference, not simple fading.
Source amnesia means remembering a fact but forgetting where you learned it. You are failing to recall the old number itself, not its source.

p: Interference means one memory gets in the way of another. Retroactive interference: new information disrupts old information. Proactive interference: old information disrupts new information.
Retro means backward, pro means forward. Ask: which memory is being blocked? If the old one is blocked, it is retroactive.

mem: Retroactive = new blocks old (backward)
Proactive = old blocks new (forward)
Decay = fading from time alone; source amnesia = forgetting where you learned it
q97.mn: Retro = Reaches back to erase old; Pro = Pushes forward to block new.
q97.trap: Mixing up the direction of interference. Find which memory is hard to recall: old blocked means retroactive.
q97.plain: It is like writing a new phone number over an old one on the same sticky note. The new writing makes the old writing hard to read.

ox: Problem-focused coping tries to change the stressor itself (make a plan, fix the problem). A loss cannot be undone, so this does not fit.
Correct. Meditation calms feelings when the situation cannot be changed. That is emotion-focused coping, and it is often a good, adaptive choice for uncontrollable stress.
The alarm stage is the body's first physiological reaction in Selye's model. It is a stage of stress, not something a person chooses to do to cope.
Learned helplessness is giving up because past stress seemed uncontrollable. Meditating to calm yourself is an active strategy, not passive giving up.

p: Coping is how we deal with stress. Problem-focused coping tackles the cause of stress. Emotion-focused coping manages the feelings the stress causes.
If the cause cannot be changed, such as a death, emotion-focused coping (meditation, talking, relaxing) is the fitting choice.

mem: Problem-focused = change the stressor
Emotion-focused = manage the feelings
Emotion-focused fits uncontrollable situations
d_6C_14.trap: Thinking emotion-focused coping is always unhealthy avoidance. It is adaptive when the stressor cannot be changed.
d_6C_14.plain: If your ball rolls over a fence you can climb it (fix the problem). If your pet has passed away, you cannot fix it, so you comfort yourself.

ox: Safety, love, and esteem are levels of Maslow's hierarchy of needs. The trap is that both theories are about needs.
Drive, incentive, and arousal are separate theories of motivation (drive-reduction, incentive, arousal theory). They are not the three needs of self-determination theory.
Correct. Self-determination theory says people thrive and feel intrinsically motivated when they have autonomy (control), competence (skill), and relatedness (connection).
Extrinsic, intrinsic, and amotivation are TYPES of motivation. They describe what drives behavior, not the needs that must be met.

p: Self-determination theory says people are most motivated from the inside (intrinsic motivation) when three needs are met. Autonomy: feeling in control of your choices. Competence: feeling skilled. Relatedness: feeling connected to others.
Outside rewards (extrinsic motivation) can weaken inner motivation if they reduce autonomy.

mem: Three needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness
Meeting them boosts intrinsic motivation
Maslow's levels are different (physiological, safety, love, esteem, self-actualization)
d_6C_23.trap: Confusing these three needs with Maslow's hierarchy levels or with types of motivation.
d_6C_23.plain: You love a video game more when you choose it yourself, you get good at it, and you play with friends.

ox: The opposite happens. The amygdala drives fear and aggression, so removing it lowers them. Assuming damage raises fear is the trap.
Vision is not lost. The animals see but fail to recognize what objects are (visual agnosia), so they treat things oddly.
The defining signs are emotional and behavioral (tameness, no fear, oral exploring). Memory deficits alone are linked more to hippocampal damage.
Correct. This is Klüver-Bucy syndrome: tameness, loss of fear, hyperorality (putting things in the mouth), and hypersexuality.

p: The amygdala is a small almond-shaped brain structure that processes fear and aggression. It sits in the temporal lobe.

Removing both temporal lobes including the amygdala causes Klüver-Bucy syndrome. Animals become calm and fearless, put everything in their mouths (hyperorality), and show increased sexual behavior (hypersexuality).

mem: Amygdala = fear and aggression
Klüver-Bucy: tameness, loss of fear, hyperorality, hypersexuality
Hippocampus = forming new declarative memories
d_6C_40.trap: Assuming amygdala damage makes animals more fearful or aggressive. It makes them tame.
d_6C_40.plain: The amygdala is like the brain's smoke alarm. Remove it and the animal is no longer scared of anything, even things it should fear.

ox: Sensory, perceptual, and motor describe taking in and acting on stimuli. They are not the parts of an emotional experience.
Conscious, preconscious, and unconscious are Freud's levels of awareness. They say nothing about how emotion is built.
Correct. Emotion has a physiological part (heart rate, sweating), a cognitive part (appraisal and feeling), and a behavioral part (expressions and actions).

Primary and secondary are used to describe appraisal (primary appraisal: is this relevant to me; secondary: can I cope) and reinforcers (primary: innately rewarding; secondary: learned). They are not a standard three-part list, and none of them are the parts of an emotion.

p: Psychologists say an emotion has three parts. Physiological: body changes like a racing heart. Cognitive: your thoughts and the feeling you have about the situation. Behavioral: what you show or do, like smiling or running away.

mem: Physiological = internal body changes
Cognitive = thoughts, appraisal, feeling
Behavioral = expressions and actions
x6C_001.trap: Picking Freud's three levels of awareness because they also come in threes.
x6C_001.plain: When you are scared: your tummy drops (body), you think 'that is a big dog' (thinking), and you run (action).

ox: Cognitive is the internal appraisal and feeling. You cannot see it directly, but a smile or fist can be seen.
Physiological means internal body responses such as heart rate and sweating. Facial and muscle actions are outward expressions, so this is the confusing near-miss.
Perception is interpreting sensory input. It is not an emotion component.
Correct. Smiling, frowning, and clenching fists are observable expressions and actions, which make up the behavioral component.

p: The behavioral component is the visible part of emotion: facial expressions, posture, gestures, and actions. Other people can observe it directly.
The physiological component is internal and automatic, like heart rate, blood pressure, and sweating.

mem: Behavioral = observable expressions and actions
Physiological = internal autonomic changes
Cognitive = inner appraisal and feeling
x6C_003.trap: Calling facial muscle movements physiological. Muscle movements you can see are behavioral.
x6C_003.plain: Behavior is what a camera can film. Physiology is what only a doctor's machine can measure.

ox: Wrong. Groupthink is when people hide doubts to keep harmony and decide badly. Here nothing suggests suppressed dissent, just a stronger version of the starting lean.
Correct. Group polarization is when discussion pushes the group further in the direction it already leaned. Moderately cautious becomes very cautious.
Wrong. Conformity to an external norm means matching an outside standard. Here the group moves on its own, further in its starting direction.
Wrong. Social loafing is putting in less effort in a group. It does not change opinions.

p: Group polarization means group discussion makes the group's average opinion more extreme in the direction it already leaned.
If members lean cautious, they become more cautious. If they lean risky, they become riskier. Groups do not always move to the middle.

mem: Polarization = initial lean becomes stronger.
Groupthink = suppressed dissent for harmony.
Social loafing = less effort in groups.
Groups do not always moderate.
d_7B_5.trap: Assuming groups always settle on a moderate view.
d_7B_5.plain: If everyone in the room mildly likes pizza, after talking it over everyone is crazy about pizza.

ox: Wrong. The contact hypothesis is about when contact between groups reduces prejudice. It does not explain boosting self-esteem by favoring your own group.
Correct. Social identity theory says belonging to a group feeds your self-concept. Favoring your own group (ingroup bias) raises self-esteem.
Wrong. The Barnum effect is accepting vague descriptions like horoscopes as personally true. It has nothing to do with groups.
Wrong. Self-perception theory says we learn our attitudes by watching our own behavior. It is not about group comparison.

p: Social identity theory says part of who you are comes from the groups you belong to. Your ingroup is your own group. An outgroup is another group.
To feel good about yourself, you may see your ingroup as better than outgroups. This is ingroup bias.

mem: Group membership feeds self-concept and self-esteem.
Ingroup bias = favoring your own group.
Outgroup homogeneity = seeing other groups as all alike.
Contact hypothesis is about reducing prejudice.
d_7B_21.trap: Missing that group membership feeds self-esteem, and grabbing a similar-sounding theory.
d_7B_21.plain: Fans think their own team is the best team. Their team doing well makes them feel good about themselves.

ox: Wrong. Instinctual drives belong to Freud's id. Cooley's idea is social, not about drives.
Wrong. Comparing to an ideal self is self-discrepancy or Rogers's idea. Cooley focuses on others' judgments, not an inner ideal. 'Only' is a clue.
Correct. Cooley's looking-glass self: we picture how others see us, picture their judgment, and build our self-concept from that.
Wrong. Reading your own body arousal belongs to emotion theories like James-Lange and Schachter-Singer.

p: Self-concept is your picture of who you are. Cooley said it comes from other people, as if they were a mirror.
There are three steps. You imagine how you look to others. You imagine how they judge you. You then feel and think about yourself based on that.

mem: Looking-glass self = imagined view of others' judgments (Cooley).
Mead = stages of role-taking (play, game, generalized other).
Rogers = ideal self vs real self.
Freud = id, ego, superego.
d_7B_22.trap: Mixing Cooley's imagined judgment with Mead's stage theory of role-taking.
d_7B_22.plain: It is like deciding you are funny because you imagine your friends laughing at your jokes.

ox: Wrong. Fundamental attribution error is blaming someone's behavior on their personality and ignoring the situation. It is about judging others, not shaping your image.
Correct. Impression management means deliberately controlling how others see you. Dressing well and stressing strengths in an interview is exactly that.
Wrong. Stereotype threat is worse performance caused by fear of confirming a negative stereotype. The candidate here is acting on purpose to look good.
Wrong. Deindividuation is losing self-awareness in a crowd or when anonymous. This candidate is very self-aware.

p: Impression management is the effort to control how other people see you. It is also called self-presentation.
It includes dress, speech and what you choose to show. It is not always lying. It can be honest and still careful.

mem: Impression management = controlling how others perceive you.
Can be honest, not only deceptive.
Deindividuation = anonymity lowers self-awareness.
Stereotype threat = fear of confirming a negative stereotype.
d_7B_25.trap: Thinking impression management always means lying.
d_7B_25.plain: It is like cleaning your room before a friend visits so they see your best side.

ox: Wrong. Fundamental attribution error is explaining behavior by personality instead of the situation. No behavior is being explained here.
Wrong. The just-world hypothesis is believing people get what they deserve. It does not spread a trait to other traits.
Correct. The halo effect is when one good trait, such as attractiveness, makes you assume other good traits like competence and honesty.
Wrong. Self-serving bias is crediting yourself for success and blaming outside causes for failure. It is about your own outcomes, not judging another person.

p: The halo effect is a thinking shortcut. One positive trait, like good looks, makes you assume the person is good at other things too.
It is a bias about one individual. The reverse, where one bad trait taints everything, is sometimes called the horn effect.

mem: Halo effect = one good trait spreads to other traits.
Attractive people are assumed more competent and honest.
Different from stereotyping, which is about a group.
Reverse = horn effect.
d_7B_26.trap: Calling it stereotyping or attribution error. The key is one trait spreading to others.
d_7B_26.plain: If a kid has the nicest handwriting, the teacher guesses the kid is also smart and well behaved.

ox: Wrong. Fixed-ratio pays after a set number of responses and gives bursts with pauses after each reward. Slot machine payouts are unpredictable, not fixed.
Wrong. Fixed-interval pays after a set time. Responding speeds up as the time nears (scalloped). Slots depend on pulls, not time.
Wrong. Variable-interval pays after unpredictable amounts of TIME. Slots depend on number of pulls, and variable-interval gives slower steady rates.
Correct. Variable-ratio pays after an unpredictable number of responses. It gives high, steady response rates and strong resistance to extinction, like slot machines.

p: A schedule of reinforcement is the rule for when a behavior gets rewarded. Ratio schedules count responses. Interval schedules count time.
Fixed means the same each time; variable means it changes. Variable-ratio produces the highest, steadiest responding and is hardest to extinguish.

mem: Variable-ratio = unpredictable number of responses, highest steady rate
Fixed-ratio = bursts then pauses
Fixed-interval = scalloped pattern
Variable-interval = slow steady rate
d_7C_6.mn: RIP: Ratio = responses (count of pulls), Interval = passing time, Pattern differs by fixed or variable.

r: Scalloped; speeds up near reward time

d_7C_6.trap: Confusing ratio (counts responses) with interval (counts time). Slots count pulls.
d_7C_6.plain: A claw machine that sometimes pays after 3 tries and sometimes after 20 keeps you pulling.

ox: Wrong. Extinction means a conditioned response fades when the CS appears without the UCS. Reacting to train noise was never conditioned, so extinction does not apply.
Correct. A decreased reaction to a repeated, harmless stimulus is habituation. The student stops noticing the trains.
Wrong. Sensitization is an increase in response, usually after an intense stimulus. Here the response decreased.
Wrong. Discrimination is responding differently to similar stimuli. The student is not telling stimuli apart, just ignoring one.

p: Habituation is a simple kind of learning where you respond less and less to a stimulus that repeats and is harmless. A stimulus is anything that triggers a reaction.
It is non-associative, meaning no pairing of two things is involved. It helps the brain ignore things that do not matter.

mem: Habituation = response decreases with repeated harmless stimulus.
Sensitization = response increases, usually after an intense stimulus.
Both are non-associative learning.
x7C_001.trap: Extinction also shows a drop in responding, but it needs a previously conditioned response.
x7C_001.plain: You hear a loud fridge hum when you first enter a house, but after a while you do not notice it at all.

ox: Correct. An intense event made the soldier more reactive to many stimuli. Increased, widespread responding is sensitization.
Wrong. Habituation is a decrease in response, and the soldier is startling more.
Wrong. Dishabituation restores a response to one stimulus that was habituated. Here many unrelated sounds trigger more startle, with no prior habituation described.
Wrong. Negative reinforcement strengthens a behavior by removing something unpleasant. No such removal is described.

p: Sensitization is an increase in responding after a strong or harmful stimulus. It is non-associative, so it does not depend on pairing two events.
It spreads: after the strong event, you react more to many different, even unrelated, stimuli.

mem: Sensitization = increased response, broad, often after an intense stimulus.
Habituation = decreased response to a repeated harmless stimulus.
Dishabituation = habituated response returns to one stimulus.
x7C_003.trap: Dishabituation sounds similar, but it concerns one stimulus that had faded, not a broad increase.
x7C_003.plain: After a scary thunderclap, you jump at every little creak in the house for a while.

ox: Wrong. The infants looked longer at the NEW face. Longer looking indicates novelty preference, not familiarity preference.
Wrong. Operant reinforcement requires a consequence after the behavior. Nothing followed looking, so no operant contingency existed.
Correct. Looking recovered for the new face, which means infants noticed it was different from the old one. They can tell the faces apart.
Wrong. Sensitization would increase looking to everything. Looking to the repeated face went down.

p: Babies cannot talk, so researchers use looking time. When a baby sees the same thing repeatedly, looking decreases. That is habituation.
If a new item makes looking rise again, that is dishabituation. It shows the baby can tell the new item from the old one.

mem: Habituation lowers looking time to a repeated stimulus.
Renewed looking to a new stimulus = discrimination.
This method tests perception in infants.
x7C_004.trap: Do not claim a preference for familiarity. Longer looking to the new item shows detection of difference.
x7C_004.plain: You get bored of the same cartoon, but perk up when a new one comes on. That shows you saw the difference.

ox: Correct. If a new stimulus can quickly bring the response back, the senses still work. So the drop came from central learning (habituation), not tired receptors.
Wrong. Habituation is a central, learned decline in responding. It is not limited to the retina.
Wrong. This describes habituation, not sensory adaptation. Adaptation is receptor-level and recovers when the stimulus stops, not through a different novel stimulus.
Wrong. Habituation needs no reward. Mere repetition of a harmless stimulus is enough.

p: Sensory adaptation happens in the receptors, the sense cells. Under constant stimulation they fire less. Example: you stop smelling a perfume.
Habituation happens in the brain and is a learned drop in response. A new stimulus can restore it right away (dishabituation), which receptor fatigue would not allow.

mem: Adaptation = receptors; habituation = brain/behavior.
Dishabituation by a novel stimulus points to habituation.
Adaptation recovers after the stimulus is removed for a while.
x7C_006.trap: Both lead to 'noticing less', so students blur them. The novel-stimulus test separates them.
x7C_006.plain: Adaptation is like a tired hand that stops feeling the watch. Habituation is like your brain deciding the watch is boring.

ox: Correct. Cooley's looking-glass self says we picture how others see and judge us, then build our self-view from that. Teachers and classmates calling her artistic shapes her self-image.
Wrong. Reaction formation is a Freudian defense that expresses the opposite of an unacceptable impulse. Nothing like that occurs here.
Wrong. Self-efficacy is belief in your ability to do a task. The story is about adopting others' views of her.
Wrong. Moratorium is a Marcia identity status of exploring options without committing. It is not how others' appraisals shape the self.

p: Cooley said we form a self-image like looking into a mirror made of other people. Three steps: imagine how others see us, imagine their judgment, and feel and react to it.
The teenager hears she is artistic and gets praise. She absorbs that view and begins to see herself as artistic.

mem: Looking-glass self = self-concept from imagined views of others (Cooley).
Mead's stages: preparatory, play, game.
Self-efficacy = belief in task ability.
Marcia statuses: diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement.
d_8A_1.trap: Confusing Cooley's looking-glass self with Mead's role-taking stages. Both are symbolic interactionism, but this story is about reflected appraisals.
d_8A_1.plain: You decide if you are funny by seeing whether your friends laugh.

ox: Wrong. The preparatory stage is imitation without understanding roles, earlier than this. This child is deliberately acting a specific role.
Correct. In Mead's play stage, children take on one specific role at a time, like doctor. They cannot yet juggle several roles.
Wrong. The game stage requires tracking many roles at once, like a team. The question says she cannot do this yet. Trap: seeing the word 'play' and choosing game.
Wrong. Formal operational is Piaget, not Mead.

p: Mead described three stages. Preparatory: imitating without understanding. Play: acting out one significant other's role at a time. Game: understanding many roles and the generalized other (society's expectations).
Playing doctor means taking one role at a time, so this is the play stage.

mem: Preparatory = imitation.
Play = one role at a time (significant others).
Game = many roles at once (generalized other).
Formal operational is Piaget, not Mead.
d_8A_3.trap: Choosing the game stage because the child is 'playing'. Count how many roles are being tracked.
d_8A_3.plain: Playing house as just the mom is the play stage. Playing a team sport where you track everyone is the game stage.

ox: Wrong. Internal locus attributes outcomes to your own effort and ability. She blames the test and the professor.
Correct. Blaming an unfair test and a disliking professor puts the cause outside herself. Doing this across many situations is an external locus of control.
Wrong. High self-efficacy is belief in your ability to affect outcomes. Blaming others does not show that.
Wrong. Self-discrepancy compares actual and ideal selves. Nothing here does.

p: Locus of control is where you believe the causes of events lie. Internal locus means your own effort and choices. External locus means luck, other people, or circumstances.
She blames the test and the professor, and does so across situations. That pattern is an external locus of control.

mem: Internal locus = I cause outcomes.
External locus = luck, others, or fate cause outcomes.
Internal links to better coping and achievement.
Self-efficacy is a different idea: belief in task ability.
d_8A_6.trap: Treating blaming others as high self-esteem. It signals external locus, not confidence.
d_8A_6.plain: If you always say the dog ate your homework, you think things happen to you, not because of you.

ox: Correct. Self-concept is the full set of beliefs and knowledge about who you are.
Wrong. Self-esteem is the judgment of how worthy you are, not the full set of beliefs. Trap: confusing description with evaluation.
Wrong. Self-efficacy is belief in your ability to succeed at specific tasks.
Wrong. Identity foreclosure is a Marcia status where someone commits to an identity without exploring options.

p: Self-concept is everything you believe about yourself: traits, roles, values. It is a description.
Self-esteem is how you feel about that self, your sense of worth. Self-efficacy is belief you can handle specific tasks.

mem: Self-concept = what I believe I am.
Self-esteem = how much I value myself.
Self-efficacy = I can do this task.
Foreclosure = commitment without exploration.
x8A_001.trap: Picking self-esteem because it sounds familiar. 'Full set of beliefs' points to self-concept.
x8A_001.plain: Self-concept is the description of you, and self-esteem is the grade you give it.

ox: Wrong. A self-schema is a set of beliefs about yourself in one area (for example, 'I am a good athlete'). It describes content, not how much you value yourself. Trap: the word 'self' appears in every option.
Correct. Self-esteem is your overall feeling of worth: how much you like and value yourself as a whole.
Wrong. Self-efficacy is confidence that you can do a specific task. You can have high efficacy in math and still low self-esteem. Trap: mixing up 'can I do it' with 'am I worth it'.
Wrong. Locus of control is whether you think outcomes come from you (internal) or from outside forces (external). It says nothing about worth.

p: Self-esteem is the feeling part of the self: your overall judgment of your own worth.
Other self ideas are narrower. A self-schema is a belief in one area. Self-efficacy is confidence in doing one task. Locus of control is who you think controls outcomes.

mem: Self-esteem = global worth judgment
Self-efficacy = confidence in a specific task
Self-schema = belief about self in one domain
Locus of control = where you place cause of outcomes
x8A_002.trap: Choosing self-efficacy because both sound like 'feeling good about yourself'. Efficacy is task-specific; esteem is global.
x8A_002.plain: Self-esteem is the grade you give yourself as a person, not the grade on one test.

ox: Wrong. A situational attribution blames circumstances outside the person. A trait explanation is the opposite.
Wrong. External causes are situational, and traits are internal. This is also not a standard label for trait explanations.
Wrong. Self-serving bias is a pattern of choosing internal causes for success and external for failure. It is not the name for every trait explanation.
Correct. A dispositional attribution places the cause inside the person: traits, abilities, effort or character.

p: An attribution is the reason you give for someone's behavior. Dispositional (internal) attributions point to the person: traits, ability, effort.
Situational (external) attributions point to circumstances, such as luck, task difficulty or other people.

mem: Dispositional = internal = traits
Situational = external = circumstances
Self-serving bias is a pattern, not an attribution type
x8B_001.trap: Mixing up the words disposition and situation, or picking self-serving bias because it sounds related.
x8B_001.plain: If your friend is late, 'he is lazy' is about him. 'Traffic was awful' is about the situation.

ox: Wrong. Low consensus and low distinctiveness with high consistency point to the person, a dispositional attribution.
Correct. Everyone acts this way (high consensus), only toward this stimulus (high distinctiveness), and reliably (high consistency). The situation is the cause.
Wrong. Low consistency means it does not happen reliably, which suggests a fluke, not a clear situational cause. Low distinctiveness also points away from the situation.
Wrong. Low consensus points to the person, and low consistency undermines any stable attribution.

p: Kelley uses three cues. Consensus: do other people act this way? Distinctiveness: does this person act this way only toward this one thing? Consistency: does it happen every time?
High-high-high points to the situation. Low consensus, low distinctiveness, high consistency points to the person.

mem: Situation = high consensus, high distinctiveness, high consistency
Person = low consensus, low distinctiveness, high consistency
Low consistency = one-time circumstance
x8B_003.trap: Mixing up which pattern means person and which means situation. Remember distinctiveness high means 'only this situation'.
x8B_003.plain: If every kid hates one scary movie, and your friend only hates that movie, and always does, the movie is the problem, not your friend.

ox: Wrong. Actor-observer bias needs a comparison of how people explain their own behavior versus others'. Only observers are judging here.
Wrong. Dissonance is discomfort from your own inconsistent beliefs and actions. Observers judging someone else's essay are not in that situation.
Wrong. A self-fulfilling prophecy needs an expectation to change someone's actual behavior. Nothing of that kind is shown.
Correct. Observers inferred an attitude matching the essay even though it was forced by a coin flip. That is correspondence bias, another name for the FAE.

p: Correspondence bias is inferring that someone's behavior matches their inner attitude, even when the situation forced that behavior.
It is the same idea as the fundamental attribution error. The coin flip is the obvious situational cause that observers ignore.

mem: Correspondence bias = FAE
Occurs even when constraints are obvious
Classic essay-assignment design
x8B_006.trap: Choosing actor-observer bias. No self-versus-other comparison exists in this design.
x8B_006.plain: An actor plays a villain in a movie, and a kid decides the actor is truly mean.

ox: Wrong. Reducing mental effort is the job of heuristics and stereotypes. Self-serving bias is motivated by feelings about the self.
Correct. Taking credit for success and deflecting blame for failure protects and boosts self-esteem.
Wrong. The bias distorts self-assessment, so it lowers accuracy.
Wrong. That fits group-serving bias, which favors the in-group. Self-serving bias is about the individual.

p: Self-serving bias is motivated reasoning. This means the brain bends explanations to feel good.
Crediting yourself for wins and blaming circumstances for losses keeps your self-worth up, even though it is less accurate.

mem: Function = protect and enhance self-esteem
Costs accuracy
Group version = group-serving bias
x8B_009.plain: It is like a kid who says 'I scored the goal' but 'the wind made me miss'. It protects his pride.

ox: Wrong. Stereotype threat affects performance of members of a stereotyped group. It does not explain observers judging a victim.
Wrong. Self-serving bias is about explaining your own successes and failures. The participants' own outcomes are not involved.
Wrong. The halo effect is one good trait spreading to other traits. It has nothing to do with fairness beliefs.
Correct. When justice cannot be restored, devaluing the victim makes the outcome seem deserved, protecting the belief that the world is fair.

p: People with a strong just-world belief expect good people to be rewarded and bad people punished.
An unpunished crime against an innocent person threatens that belief. Lowering your opinion of the victim fixes the threat in your mind.

mem: Just-world belief → blame or devalue victims
Strongest when justice cannot be restored
It restores a sense of fairness
x8B_011.trap: Choosing self-serving bias just because a bias is named. Ask whose outcome is being explained.
x8B_011.plain: If a good kid gets hurt and no one is blamed, a child who believes in fairness decides the kid must have been not so good.

ox: Correct. She earned it through residency and certification, so it is an achieved status.
Wrong. Ascribed statuses are assigned at birth or involuntarily, like age or race. Surgeon is earned.
Wrong. Master status is a status that dominates how others see a person. Nothing suggests surgeon overrides all her other statuses.
Wrong. Primary describes a type of group (close, personal), not a type of status.

p: A status is a position in society. An achieved status is gained through effort, choices, or merit, such as earning a degree.
Ascribed statuses are assigned without effort. A master status is any status that overshadows all the others.

mem: Achieved = earned.
Ascribed = assigned at birth or involuntarily.
Master = dominates how others see you.
x8C_001.trap: Do not choose master just because the job is prestigious. The stem needs a status type about how it was gained.
x8C_001.plain: Earning a black belt takes training. Being born in March does not.

ox: Wrong. A role set is the group of roles that go with one status, like a teacher's roles with students and parents. It does not mean a dominant label.
Wrong. A criminal record comes from his own actions, so it is not ascribed. Trap: assuming an imposed label means ascribed.
Wrong. A reference group is a group used as a standard to compare yourself against. It is not a status.
Correct. His ex-offender status overshadows his degree and work history. A status that dominates all others is a master status.

p: A master status is the one status that overrides all others and shapes how people treat you. It can be positive or negative.
How it was gained does not matter. What makes it master is that it dominates. This one is achieved, since it came from his own actions.

mem: Master status = dominates all other statuses.
It can be ascribed or achieved.
Role set = roles tied to one status.
x8C_002.trap: A label that feels imposed is not automatically ascribed. Judge it by how it was gained.
x8C_002.plain: If everyone only calls you the kid who broke the window, that label hides everything else about you.

ox: Wrong. A status set is ALL the statuses one person holds (professor, mother, citizen). The trap is mixing up 'many statuses' with 'many roles inside one status'.
Correct. A role set is the group of roles that go with ONE status. The status 'professor' brings teaching, advising and committee roles.
Wrong. Role strain is stress from clashing demands inside a role. The stem lists behaviors but shows no stress, so do not add tension that is not there.
Wrong. A master status is the one status that overshadows all others in how people see you. Nothing here says her job dominates her identity.

p: A status is a position in society, like professor or mother. A role is the set of behaviors expected from someone in that position.
One status usually has several roles attached. That bundle is the role set. All the statuses one person holds together make the status set.

mem: Status = position; role = expected behavior
Role set = many roles, ONE status
Status set = many statuses, ONE person
x8C_003.trap: Students swap 'role set' and 'status set'. Ask: is it many roles for one position, or many positions for one person?
x8C_003.plain: Think of a video game character (status: 'knight'). The knight has several jobs: fight, guard the gate, protect the king. Those jobs together are the role set.

ox: Wrong. Achieved statuses are earned or chosen, like being a doctor. The prince did nothing to get his title.
Wrong. 'Instrumental' describes group ties built around a goal or task. It is not a type of status, so it is a vocabulary distractor.
Correct. An ascribed status is assigned at birth or by others, without effort. Royal title, sex and ethnicity are classic examples.
Wrong. Role exit is leaving a role. He has not left anything, and it is not a status type.

p: A status is a social position. An ascribed status is given to you, usually at birth, and you cannot easily change it. An achieved status is something you earn or choose through effort.
Examples: ascribed is age, sex, race, royal birth. Achieved is being a surgeon or a college graduate.

mem: Ascribed = assigned, no effort
Achieved = earned or chosen
Birth-based titles are ascribed
x8C_004.trap: The prince will later perform duties, which tempts you toward 'achieved'. The question asks how he got the status, not what he does with it.
x8C_004.plain: Ascribed is like the color of your eyes, you were handed it. Achieved is like a trophy you won.

ox: Correct. Status inconsistency means a person holds statuses with very different prestige. Physician is high, her stigmatized group membership is low, so people treat her in mixed ways.
Wrong. Role exit means leaving a role. She is still a physician, so no exit happened.
Wrong. Role strain is competing demands within ONE role. Her problem is unequal prestige between TWO statuses.
Wrong. Her physician status is achieved, but 'achieved master status' does not name a clash between statuses. The clash is the point of the question.

p: Every status has a level of prestige, or social respect. Status inconsistency happens when one person has statuses with very different prestige levels.
Others may then react unpredictably, respecting one status while looking down on another.

mem: Status inconsistency = mismatched prestige across statuses
Role strain = one role, competing demands
Role conflict = two roles, competing demands
x8C_006.trap: Role strain sounds right because she feels pressure. But strain is about demands, not prestige mismatch.
x8C_006.plain: It is like being the school's best player but also the new kid nobody sits with. Some people cheer, others ignore you.

ox: Wrong. Functionalism is macro-level and asks how social structures keep society stable. It does not focus on how individuals read a single gesture.
Correct. Symbolic interactionism says meaning comes from shared and negotiated interpretation of symbols, so one handshake can mean respect or challenge.
Wrong. Conflict theory is macro-level and focuses on power and inequality. Nothing here involves competition over resources.
Wrong. Demographic transition theory describes changes in birth and death rates, not everyday interaction.

p: This is a micro-level theory. It studies how people create meaning through symbols (words, gestures, objects) in face-to-face interaction.
Meaning is not built in. It is negotiated, so the same gesture can be read differently by different people.

mem: Symbolic interactionism = micro, meaning from symbols
Functionalism and conflict theory = macro
Same symbol can carry different meanings
d_9A_3.trap: Defaulting to a macro theory. The key clue is individuals interpreting the same gesture differently.
d_9A_3.plain: A thumbs-up can mean 'great' in one country and be rude in another. The meaning lives in people's heads.

ox: Wrong. This describes biological determinism, where categories are fixed facts discovered by society. Constructionism says the opposite.
Correct. Social constructionism holds that categories like adolescence get meaning from collective agreement and vary across societies and eras.
Wrong. This describes rational choice theory, where people weigh personal costs and benefits.
Wrong. This is a narrow conflict-theory claim. The word 'only' is a warning sign.

p: Social constructionism says many things we treat as real, such as money or adolescence, get their meaning because people agree on it together.
Because meanings are made by people, they differ across cultures and time. Constructed does not mean fake. These ideas still have real effects.

mem: Meanings are created by shared agreement
Categories vary across cultures and history
Constructed does not mean unreal
d_9A_6.trap: Thinking 'constructed' means 'fake'. Also avoid options with 'only' or 'fixed'.
d_9A_6.plain: Rules of a playground game exist because the kids agree on them. Different playgrounds have different rules.

ox: Wrong. A subculture is a group with distinct practices that lives alongside the mainstream. It is not defined by opposing it. The trap is that both words describe 'different' groups.
Wrong. A reference group is a group you compare yourself to when judging your own behavior or status. It says nothing about rejecting values.
Wrong. A primary group is a small, close, long-lasting group like family. It is defined by closeness, not opposition.
Correct. A counterculture deliberately rejects and opposes mainstream norms and values.

p: A subculture shares the main culture but has its own tastes or practices, such as a hobby community.
A counterculture goes further. It actively rejects the main culture's norms and builds a way of life against them. The key word is opposition.

mem: Subculture = different, coexists
Counterculture = opposes mainstream values
Reference group = comparison standard
Primary group = close, lasting ties
d_9A_20.trap: Picking subculture because it sounds like the general term. 'Deliberately rejects' signals counterculture.
d_9A_20.plain: A subculture is a club at school with its own handshake. A counterculture is a club that says the school rules are wrong and makes its own.

ox: Wrong. McDonaldization is about standardization and rules, which squeeze out spontaneity. The trap is picking the opposite of the concept.
Wrong. The concept actually relies on technology to increase control. It does not describe resisting it.
Wrong. Rationalization spreads formal organizations and bureaucracy rather than shrinking them.
Correct. Ritzer's four features are efficiency, predictability, calculability, and control.
